She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to rise and speak to my private member's bill which would establish a national day of remembrance and action on violence against women, and which has received all party support in this House of Commons.
This bill is being co-sponsored by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women and also by my colleague, the member for Halifax.
An official day of remembrance and action on violence against women to be commemorated every December 6 is an appropriate, meaningful and positive memorial to the 14 young women who were so tragically killed in Montreal on December 6, 1989.
I am pleased to have the support also of Suzanne Edwards, the mother of one of the victims of the massacre, who herself is now very active on the issue of gun control. She serves as an inspiration to all Canadians to first mourn and then to work for change in our society.
The man who murdered the 14 young women separated the women from the men in the classroom and systematically shot the women. He believed that because they were engineering students they were feminists, and
he saw them as women who had stepped outside of their rightful place. He put an end to young promising lives, lives filled with hard work, joy and plans for the future. He did not see these young women as human beings. All he saw was that they were women and that they had stepped out of what he considered to be their traditional role.
Unfortunately, there are people in Canada who share that outlook on life. There are people who see rape victims not as people who are suffering from a trauma, but as women who "deserved it". There are people who think that wife beating is something to laugh at or nothing to be concerned about. Some believe that the woman deserved it, like 25 per cent of the children who lived at a shelter and said it was appropriate for a man to hit a woman if the house were messy.
There is a deep and serious problem in our society, one that I do think Canadians are slowly starting to come to terms with. Women are now reporting violent crimes to police more often than they did in the past. Some people in our society think violence is increasing, but I do not think so. I remember 20 years ago when a badly beaten woman appeared on my doorstep with two very small children, looking for a safe haven. At that time there were no shelters for battered women. Our society did not acknowledge wife battering as a problem. The police did not charge husbands with any crime. Before that, wife beating was a perfectly legal activity; women could not get a divorce on the grounds of assault or because their husbands had beaten them to a pulp. That was not considered a good enough reason. It was a private shame to be hidden, lied about and suffered in silence.
These attitudes still run through our society as an undercurrent in the 1990s but committed groups of people have set up shelters. They are talking about the issues. They are making educational videos and anti-violence television commercials. They are protesting against unfair court decisions.

June 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
This bill is designed to help that work by focusing attention on the facts of violence against women. I hope that the media will participate by having special issues of newspapers and magazines or TV and radio programs on violence against women at least on that day.
The more we talk about it, learn the facts and teach our children and society that violence against women is wrong and never justifiable, the more progress we will make as a society toward a fair and equitable community in Canada.
The national day of remembrance and action could be a day on which people are encouraged to donate time or money to shelters for battered women and to rape relief centres, and to talk about the attitudes and circumstances that allow violence against women to continue.
We should be aware of violence against women every day of the year, but at least we can start with one day.
One hundred women a year are killed as a result of domestic violence and a woman is raped every 17 minutes in Canada. This horrible situation warrants at least one day of prevention and education.
One in 10 women is or has been battered by the man with whom she lives or did live. Every 17 minutes a sexual assault is committed in Canada and 90 per cent of the victims are female.
Between 63 and 83 per cent of female victims are assaulted by someone they know and trust. Incidence of assault is far greater for aboriginal women and disabled women. Forty-eight per cent of Canadians reported that they personally knew of situations in which women were physically assaulted.
A Canada-wide survey in 1985 found that fewer than 40 per cent of female sexual assault victims and less than half of wife assault victims had made a police report. Studies show that women's reluctance to report violent attacks against them is related to the fear of retaliation that would result in further violence or death. It is also related to a lack of confidence in the police and the courts, and to feelings of shame and embarrassment. The more we talk about violence and its causes, the
more confidence it will give women who have been assaulted to report it to the police and to take action.
The physical effects of this violence include broken bones, internal injuries, bruises, black eyes, bums, bites, lacerations, knife wounds, gun wounds and death. The psychological effects are low self-esteem, constant fear for her own safety and the safety of her children, loss of control and isolation.
Women who have been sexually assaulted are approximately five times more likely to have a nervous breakdown, six times more likely to attempt suicide and eight times as likely to commit suicide or die prematurely. Physical and sexual abuse may lead to drug and alcohol abuse.
The sheer volume of female victimization makes it unlikely that these incidents are independent of our system of values and attitudes or that the perpetrators are all aberrant or insane individuals. Perpetrators overwhelmingly hold views about sex roles of male authority and female compliance, and believe they have the right to control persons with less status than themselves. Our society is not telling them that they are wrong.
We live in a society which has tolerated incest, sexual assault and wife beating for centuries.
It is a problem of global proportions. Sexual assault and wife beating have been used to control the behaviour and the sexuality of women not only by the men who resort to violence, but by the society which ignores it.
Rape victims are still raked over the coals not only by the courts but often by the families and by their own friends: "What were you wearing? Why were you out so late? Why did you trust him? Could you not see it coming? But he is your husband, you owe it to him." It is as if human rights are suspended if a person is wearing a particular piece of clothing.
Nowhere in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have I seen a clause that says one's right to security of the person is suspended based on the article of clothing one is wearing. This argument seeks to make women responsible for the violent acts of others. Sexual assault is not about sex; it is not about sexual desirability; it is about power. It is about a man believing he has the right to force something on a woman against her will. It has happened to women of all ages, from babies of three
June 3, 1991

weeks of age to 96 year-old women. Women with little or no power are especially targeted. Disabled women and aboriginal women, the women whom our society allows to be discriminated against, are at a special risk of violence.
It happens in war time, it happens in peace time. People have said there is a war being waged against women all the time. Racism, discrimination against the disabled and all forms of discrimination and oppression merge with the sickness of sexism to intensify the hatred and violence against disadvantaged women.
Women in all strata of society are abused. Why should we be afraid on our own streets, the streets for which we pay taxes? Why should we be afraid in our own homes? We are most likely to be assaulted in our own homes by someone whom we know and trust.
Studies of male college students in Canada and the U.S. show that one third of these students said they would rape a woman if they thought they could get away with it. In the U.S., 15 per cent of college women had been raped within the legal definition of rape.
Research shows that the public perceives physical and sexual assault against women to take place mainly among the poor and among those with little formal education, and committed by deviant individuals. Unless grievous bodily injury results, these injuries are not regarded as causing long term harm to the victim. Many of these victims are seen to be the authors of their own attack because they are seen as too provocative, too sexy, too angry or too imprudent.
We lack an understanding of the social and economic circumstances and of the threats of more violence or death that keep battered women from leaving abusive situations. Most people do not realize that many of the women killed are murdered by former husbands and lovers after the women have left the abusive situation. All of our society must take responsibility to help women in crisis.
Some people even believe violence against women is natural because men tend to be stronger than women. I think this takes a very dim view of men. If one in ten women is battered, then nine out of ten men do not batter.
Most men are responsible and caring. Violence against women is a learned and an unnatural behaviour. It is based upon the premise that men should be able to control the lives of the women with whom they are
Private Members' Business
intimate. An example of this is Jean-Guy Tremblay who tried to force Chantal Daigle to bear his child and was violent and abusive toward her. It is worth noting that this man continued his violent behaviour toward other women who came into his life after Chantal Daigle refused to see him any longer.
Men who are violent most often do not stop simply at physical abuse. They may bum or destroy a favourite picture or possession, kill the woman's pets, or threaten violence toward her children. Battered women may live with psychological terror, never knowing when the next outbreak will be, or for what inane reason.
The man often makes her quit her job or gets her fired by harassing her at work. He isolates her from her workplace, her family and her friends. He tries to have complete control over her life and thoughts.
Similarly, sexual assault is a matter of control.
The woman's will is overrun, what she wants does not count and she is humiliated and violated in a v/ay that is unmatched by any other experience.
People have talked about having their homes, their territory, robbed and the violation that they feel as a person when this happens. Can you imagine what it is like when it is your own body rather than your home and your possessions?
The lack of understanding many Canadians have about this issue makes me want to weep. But instead of, or maybe in addition to, weeping, I want to do something concrete about it.
My bill is non-partisan, one of the very few bills of this nature ever to reach the House of Commons. We have left the days when politicians simply joked about this issue. Today, most of us can co-operate on an issue as serious as this.
All of society pays for violence against women. We pay in health bills, in the court system and in penal institutions. Studies show that 80 per cent of women in Canadian jails are victims of sexual and physical abuse. Half of young offenders were exposed to domestic violence.
With few economic options, women who leave abusive situations often end up on social assistance.
How long are we going to put up with the violent abuse of our mothers, sisters, and daughters? It is wrong. It must change. The time for change is long past due. We

Private Members' Business
must join together, men and women, to prevent this violence.
As the Church Council on Justice and Corrections and the Canadian Council on Social Development have stated in their document "Family Violence in a Patriarchal Culture", family violence does not happen in a vacuum. Social circumstances support it and allow it to continue.
I urge men to participate in social change by speaking out when they hear others make derogatory comments about women, comments which rob women of their dignity and their humanity.
We can all help our neighbour who is being abused. We can give our time and money to groups and organizations which help survivors of violence. We can educate our society. We can make change.
We can press for policies that give women economic options so that they can achieve meaningful equality. Once all of society accepts women and men as equal human beings, that the place of women and men is where they want to be and not some role simply designated to them at birth, that is when violence against women will no longer be tolerated and may no longer occur.
Judy Chicago, a well known feminist artist, expressed her vision of a future without violence, a world in which both female and male are valued and respected. She said:
And then all that has divided us will merge
And then compassion will be wedded to power
And then softness will come to a world that is harsh and unkind
And then both men and women will be gentle
And then both women and men will be strong
And then no person will be subject to another's will.
I want to thank the House for its support of this bill. I want to thank Suzanne Edward, the mother of Anne Marie Edward who was killed in the massacre, and I want to thank women's organizations and groups in every region of this country which have supported this effort.
Together I know that we can make a difference. We can do no less.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to say I support this bill designate a national day of remembrance and action on violence against women, to be held on December 6 of each year, the anniversary of the slaughter of 14 young women at the University of Montreal in 1989.
Members of all parties have acknowledged the significance of this tragic event in the lives of Canada's men and women. Every year on December 6, we will think back to that sad day in our history and we will remember the victims. Those who experienced the events of that day will relive the shock, horror and anger that they felt. We will remember the candlelight vigil in the snow for 14 young women who were killed simply because they were women. We will remember the grief and sympathy we felt for their families and friends.
This bill guarantees that future generations will also remember. It ensures that the memory of 14 brave women will always remain with us. In fact, their spirit lives on, if we consider what has been done since the tragedy at the Ecole polytechnique to eliminate violence against women. Everywhere in Canada, the initial shock was followed by an increased awareness of the constant threat of violence against women in our society.
People are now determined to act. The loss of these young women has made people realize there is a need for accelerating and co-ordinating efforts to eliminate violence against women.
As we become more aware of the extent of the problem, we realize this is not an easy task. Violence against women is deeply rooted in a social process that stresses the traditional roles of men and women, the so-called stereotypes. These stereotypes can become apparent in many ways, ranging from sexual harassment to mental cruelty, from sexual assault to murder.
Attempts to deal with the problem of violence against women must consider the social, economic and political structures that today confine women in a position of inequality. At the same time, we must keep looking for ways to increase the opportunities and choices open to women.
June 3, 1991

I think that if we want to deal with or try to deal with the problem of violence against women, we must base our efforts on four principles.
First, we must take a co-ordinated, many-facetted approach. This approach is reflected in the $136 million initiative on family violence announced by this government in February. It establishes a partnership between six federal departments and agencies with common concerns in this area.
But there is more. No single government can deal effectively with the problem of violence against women without the co-operation of other levels of government, without the interest and expertise of other parties, including those who work directly with the victims as well as the researchers, women's groups, service clubs, educators, unions and professional associations. Creating and strengthening alliances between these parties is one of the objectives of the family violence initiative.
The provinces and territories play a key role in our efforts to combat violence against women. Last year, federal, provincial and territorial ministers responsible for the status of women issued a declaration on violence against women at Lake Louise in Alberta. At their annual meeting, to be held two weeks from now in Newfoundland, the ministers will discuss the strategies designed by their respective governments following this declaration. They will seek ways to integrate and co-ordinate their activities and those of municipalities, the private sector and non-govemmental organizations.
The second principle is the need for examining the underlying causes of violence against women. Causes are deeply rooted and the solutions are complex. Yet, little research was done on the underlying causes of violence against women. Before we can find effective long term solutions, we must determine the underlying cause of violent behaviour.
Professional organizations such as the Canadian Association of university teachers (CAUT) are among those which have been spearheading the action. Our government is presently working with CAUT to set up centres of excellence to promote research on the underlying causes of violence against women.
Private Members' Business
Better data and better research will help develop effective solutions relating to prevention, which I consider as the third component in this approach.
While it is important to help those who are presently victims of violence, more needs to be done yet to protect would-be victims. More needs to be done to fight the widespread attitudes that perpetuate violence against women. More needs to be done in the way of channeling our innovative imagination and our resources towards durable long term solutions.
One thing we could do to start with is change attitudes in our families and schools. In a number of schools, the approach used to tackle the problem of violence against women is to teach children some conflict resolution skills as an alternative to violence. Also, the Canadian Teachers' Federation has launched the "Thumb" project with the financial assistance of the Family Violence Prevention Division of Health and Welfare Canada to encourage discussion in the classroom as well as activities aimed at preventing violence.
Fourth, we must consider the challenge of preventing violence against women in the broader context of a program to empower women.
As long as women remain afraid of violence, they cannot become fully equal. As long as there are women beaten up by their spouses, women sexually assaulted on dates and women harassed at the workplace, women will be deprived of the fundamental right to personal safety.
Mr. Speaker, our government is trying to free women from violence and the fear of violence. Last month, in the Speech from the Throne, this government announced the appointment of a blue ribbon panel of Canadian men and women to inquire into the various dimensions of the problem of violence against women and suggest innovative solutions.
This announcement provides an opportunity to put in place an innovative, responsive and flexible system to try and find solutions. The Minister responsible for the Status of Women, the hon. Mary Collins, asked women's organizations across the country as well as the provinces and territories to make suggestions on what the mandate and membership of this committee should be.
The committee will also benefit from the invaluable recommendations contained in the soon to be tabled report from the sub-committee on the Status of Women. As you will know, the sub-committee has heard, over the

June 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
past six months, the testimonies of about 35 groups representing a wide cross-section of Canadian men and women concerned about violence against women.
Mr. Speaker, this government is determined to act on this. Things will not change overnight, not even within a week or a year. While I fully support this bill, I have to say, that I hope this national day of remembrance can be taken off our calendars in the future and that the day will come when there is no need for a day dedicated to action on violence against women. I am convinced that, with the help and cooperation of the thousands of Canadian men and women who have voiced their determination to eradicate this plague from our society, some day this problem will disappear.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure I stand today to support this private member's bill initiated by the member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
I want to take a moment to pay a tribute to the member for New Westminster-Burnaby and say that in our time here in this Chamber, over the last two and a half years, in spite of political differences and differences in political philosophy, I can truly say that one of the people who has taught me that sisterhood is powerful is the member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
I give this bill very strong support. To say that it is an idea whose time has come is to understate the case. None of us who lived through that terrible night, December 6, 1989, will ever forget the horror of the deaths of those young women in the prime of life, cut down because they were women. None of us will forget the shock we felt at the fact that this kind of senseless atrocity could take place in a country which, in spite of all its difficulties, we all felt somehow was better than that. None of us will every forget the numbness and then the pain that followed when we realized that this terrible incident had, indeed, taken place and that those young lives had been snuffed out.
One of the things we can do to put some meaning into that senseless atrocity is to support this bill. I am delighted that we have put down the cudgels of partisanship on this matter and that all parties are supporting this bill, and its quick passage.
I spoke some weeks ago with Madam Susanne Edward, mentioned by my colleague from New Westminster- Burnaby. She spoke of the necessity to give meaning to what had happened, to give meaning to those lives being cut off in their prime. Nothing could be more essential to this meaning than bringing the issue of violence against women into the national spotlight.
We all lived through the horror of December 6, 1989, but horror is a daily occurrence for literally thousands of Canadian women. Every day begins with the anticipation of an attack, the fear of an attack, the worry that an attack may take place, and often that attack will come from the person closest to her.
We have talked a lot about the causes and the reasons for the increasing violence against women in our own society and in western society in general. The hon. parliamentary secretary, and I compliment her as well on her speech on this bill, talked about the fact that we do not have the empirical data, the research that we need to tell us what the reasons and the causes are for this horror that takes place.
What we do have is something that is actually also rooted in women's experience, and it is what we call anecdotal evidence, of women talking to each other in their homes, in women's centres, in classrooms. Not that this is not valid evidence, but we need hard scientific proof to show us what the different causes are. We all know, through this anecdotal evidence, that a cause of some of the violence against women is alcoholism. We all know that a cause is bad economic circumstances. We all know that a cause is the cycle of violence. In other words, someone who was abused as a child or saw his mother being abused or saw women being abused has a very strong chance of growing up to be an abuser himself.
These are not the only causes. There are other causes that we know little or nothing about. We also do not know the intertwining linkages of these causes, the tinderbox effect which sets it off.
Just this past weekend, yesterday as a matter of fact, I was in my apartment in Halifax.
June 3, 1991

My telephone rang. It was a woman who had been a client of mine. She had experienced an outbreak of violence by her partner on Saturday night. She was upset, she was still in a certain amount of pain-both physical pain and emotional pain-and most particularly, she was ashamed.
I became angry on the telephone, trying very carefully to make her understand that I was not angiy with her but angry at the situation where the victim bears the shame for someone else's act.
All women are aware of this whole aura of "victimology" that violence against women has set up, whether that violence is abusive in the non-sexual sense or abusive in the sexual sense. We are all aware that the general accepted theory in our society for hundreds of years has been that if a woman is assaulted, somehow it is her fault.
This has become so ingrained in our society that women themselves believe it. It was that belief that I could hear in her voice that set off a chain reaction in me, and I got a little bit preachy, I am afraid, and said: "Look, stop thinking that it is your fault. It is not your fault. It does not matter what you did, no one has the right to hit you".
No matter how many times we say that, no matter how many times counsellors in transition houses and social workers and doctors and all of the various professionals and experts who work in this field say that, deep down in every abused woman's heart and mind is the belief that: "Yes, it is my fault".
Again, we have to get at the root causes that take a woman's self-image and drive it down to the level where she can be convinced to believe that canard.
Another of the reasons that I support this bill so strongly is that it is another spotlight on the question of violence bringing the issue into the public forum of discussion. As a result of this, people will finally be made to understand that this is not something that happens to some fringe group, that it is not something that happens to some under-class of society, that violence against women takes place at every level, in every economic bracket, in every social strata, in every educational strata in our country. No woman is free from fear of violence in Canada, and if she thinks she is I can only say she is
Private Members' Business
misguided. Every woman sitting in this House today knows that and knows it viscerally.
I am happy to say that I think a great many of the men sitting in this House at least acknowledge it intellectually-
There is a continuum of violence against women. It begins in some cases with sexual harassment, with demeaning cracks, with jokes that we are supposed to accept and take in good spirit, and runs the gamut to actual physical beating and death. We have seen too much of this in this country. We have sacrificed hundreds of women as we refused to face this question head on and deal with it.
I hope and I pray, along with all of my female colleagues in this House and my male colleagues as well, that taking this day, December 6, and making it a day of remembrance but even more a day of action will start the kind of action that we need, that we must have in this country to ensure that women, and most particularly our daughters, will be able to walk out of their homes and into their classrooms and into their jobs without fear.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to support the motion of the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
No member of this House will ever forget the day we received the tragic news from Ecole Polytechnique. None of us will ever forget the wave of grief and anger that swept the country when we learned that a lone gunman had brutally taken the lives of 14 young women engineering students.
All members of this House were united in expressing our profound sense of loss and horror and in extending our condolences to the families and loved ones of those women whose lives, which had shown such promise, were exterminated without any provocation by a young man insanely jealous of the achievement of women in a non-traditional field.
December 6, 1989, is a day that many Canadians, and particularly women in Canada, will recall vividly for all their lives. It was one of those searing events when a story we hear on the news manages to hit home with a sense of personal loss and tragedy.
For all Canadians, women and men, who had believed that we lived in a progressive society, a society of

Private Members' Business
compassion and the pursuit of equality, the event has been a reminder of how far we have yet to go.
For women across Canada who saw, in the brutal slaying, an extreme example of the terror and violence inflicted on women every day, often in more subtle ways but sometimes with blood and death, the event has left deep wounds.
For those who lived through the terror, for those who knew the young women personally, the event has also left deep wounds. This legislation is about healing those wounds.
We cannot bring back to life those 14 young women, but we can ensure that their deaths will not be forgotten. In our remembrance we can ensure that their loss will continue to call us to action. Our remembrance will rally us to renew our efforts to eradicate violence against women in this country. We will vow to rededicate our efforts to ensure that violence against women will not be tolerated.
Let no one forget that the capacity for such brutal misogyny exists in our society. Let no one forget that acts of violence, less sensational, less publicized, but every bit as pernicious, occur every day in our streets and even in our homes.
In the same year that these 14 lost their lives, another 100 women in Canada were murdered by their partners. These deaths are part of a much larger phenomenon that covers a range of violence: murder, physical assault, sexual assault, psychological abuse and emotional abuse. These are all examples of violence against women and we are just beginning to acknowledge the enormous scope of this violence in our society.
We know, from a 1981 Winnipeg study, that more than 6 in 10 female victims will be assaulted by someone they know. We know from Battered but not Beaten-Preventing Wife Abuse in Canada, a 1987 publication of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, that at least one woman in 10 is battered by her male partner.
These tragic statistics are available to us, but one of the most serious problems when dealing with violence against women is that there is so much we do not know. Much of the violence goes unrecorded, much of the data is incomplete. Some victims fear the consequences of continuing to live in their homes after reporting a family member who has abused them. Some victims think they
would do best to forget. They try to bury the violence deep in their thoughts and deny its existence. They do not fully understand the deep-seated trauma that such violence inflicts and that will, in all likelihood, stay with them the rest of their lives.
By recognizing December 6 as a national day of remembrance and action on violence against women, Parliament will send a signal to those women. As members of this House, we will be telling them that we know such violence takes place, that we know of their trauma and that they are not alone in their suffering. We will be inviting them to join us as we move forward together to eradicate violence against women from Canadian society.
We will be sending a signal to all Canadians through our solidarity of purpose in ensuring that violence against women shall not be ignored. We will be helping to create a social environment in which attitudes toward women which promote such violence must wither and die.
The idea of designating the date of the Ecole Polytechnique disaster as a day of remembrance and action has wide support. It is being supported by members from all sides of the House and it responds to recommendations that have come from women's groups across the country, as well as from the many individuals who were touched by the tragedy.
The National Council of Women of Canada and a number of other national women's groups recommended December 6 be proclaimed a national day of mourning.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women proposed that the day be set aside as a day of recognition of women victims at the hands of male violence.
I commend the hon. member for New Westminster- Burnaby for tabling a bill that is not content to let December 6 be solely a day of remembrance. It will also be a day of constructive action. Already we have seen many examples of how the tragedy has galvanized Canadians to act.
At universities and colleges across Canada students and faculty are speaking out against practices that contribute to the sexist environment in which violence against women festers. We are seeing the establishment
June 3, 1991

of sexual harassment policies and committees, as well as status of women offices and women's centres.
The federal government has shown leadership and vision through its commitment to Canada's first national inquiry into violence against women and its $136 million renewal of the family violence initiative.
The tragedy of December 6 has also led to action by fostering a renewed commitment to opening career opportunities to women, particularly with respect to science and engineering.
The Canadian Federation of University Women, the Canadian Council of Engineers Memorial Foundation, Societe Alfred Dallaire, and Ecole Polytechnique are among the organizations, institutions and corporations that have established scholarships in memory of the victims.
Many of these scholarships are designed to encourage women to pursue careers in engineering, the discipline studied by 12 of the Ecole Polytechnique victims. These scholarships will help to break down the barriers that have prevented women from assuming full equality in our society.
When we break down the stereotypes and open nontraditional careers to women, we undermine the attitudes of sexism that can give rise to violence.
Our efforts to eradicate violence against women cannot be separated from our concern for economic equality of women. The two are bound together.
When we provide women with economic freedom through employment equity and measures to integrate work and family responsibilities, we provide women with the freedom to leave abusive situations. We again contribute to breaking down the stereotypes.
At the same time, we will never fully succeed in removing the obstacles to full equality so long as violence against women continues to plague our society.
When the basic right to security of the person is denied, no one can participate as an equal. Violence and the fear of violence are depriving women in Canada and around the world of their ability to achieve equality.
Private Members' Business
No one can doubt the persistence of violence against women, but at the same time no one should doubt our determination to eliminate it.
By setting aside December 6, we will have occasion each year in Canada to pause and consider what we have done to eradicate this evil, and what remains to be done.
We will have occasion to mourn those whom we have lost to violence, and honour those who show their determination to work toward equality for women.
One example of that determination came to light this past year when one of the prestigious Canada Scholarships was awarded to Nathalie Provost.
Nathalie was among the women wounded by the gunman at Ecole Polytechnique. At the Canada Scholarship Assembly at Ecole Polytechnique, she declared: "He did not win."
Determined words. They are words that speak on behalf of the women engineering students at Ecole Polytechnique. A year after the tragedy, a record 222 women, a quarter of the class, enrolled as first-year engineering students.
The words "he did not win" are a call to action as much as they are a declaration of how women have overcome the Montreal tragedy. They are words that speak for women everywhere, women who face the threat of violence in their lives, on the streets and even in their homes every day of the year.
It is a fitting memorial, a day to assess and remember and look at the issue of violence against women. It is a particularly fitting memorial because these young women were the victims of a young man, himself a twisted product of a violent father whose attitudes affected his son.
Such sick attitudes and actions should not be tolerated in our society. Their consequences are terrible.
As members of Parliament, it is our duty to ensure that the declaration of Nathalie Provost rings true for all women.

Mr. Speaker, I think you would find the House disposed to complete this matter and put it to a vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that I fully support the bill. We are looking forward to its passage with the agreement of all parties in the House of Commons.
We need to see more of this in Private Members' Business. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today for third reading of Bill C-15, an act to provide for certain matter respecting official languages, employees'

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
pensions and labour relations in connection with the transfer of certain airports.
Bill C-15 will allow the government to proceed with negotiations that are under way, to effect those transfers and fulfil the objectives of the government's policy in this matter, keeping in mind that this bill deals exclusively with employee related matters.
As all members are aware, the government's objectives from the beginning were to allow the airports to better serve local community interests, to enhance regional economic development potential, and to permit the national airport system to operate in a more cost-effective and commercial manner.
This policy aims to enhance the efficient commercial operation of federal airports through a more locally responsive management structure.
This government's vision is that this new structure will allow airports to respond quickly to changing needs and market forces with innovative ideas.
The local airport authorities, or LAAs will benefit from increased flexibility that will enable them to take advantage of the entrepreneurial opportunities that present themselves. They will be in a positive position to directly contribute to regional development initiatives.
The government set out very clear principles for these transfers in the original policy statement and the supplementary principles which set out the conditions under which airports would be transferred to local authorities.
It might be worth repeating that under the government's principles, permanent employees must be offered work by the local airport authorities in a job with pay and benefits comparable to what they received while employed by Transport Canada. Airport employees will be properly looked after.
Airport staff are dedicated and skilled professionals. This bill, along with the principles of the transfer process, will ensure that they are treated fairly and equally.
These local airport authorities will be non-profit organizations. Current and forecast net revenue generated by the airport must be guaranteed to the government, along with a share of the increased revenue produced by the local airport authority.
Passage of this bill should greatly contribute to allaying any concerns that affected airport site employees may have by dealing with their major questions concerning pensions, benefits, and collective agreements.
This airport transfer legislation would also ensure that the LAAs continue to provide bilingual services to the public at former federal airports.
Negotiations are well advanced with local airport authorities in Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver and Montreal. The signature of former transfers in these communities could take place as early as this fall. This House may already be aware that serious interest in airport transfers is also evident in such communities as Moncton, Quebec City, St. Foy, Windsor, Thunder Bay, Winnipeg, and Kamloops.
In summary, this bill, which will allow the government to proceed with the transfer of airports to locally established airport authorities, will allow Transport Canada to be in an even better position to focus its energies and resources on the vital aspects of transportation in Canada.
In closing, I just want to thank all hon. members for their interest in this bill and in this process.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to address this legislation before the House at third reading. It is the bill which will transfer the authority of airports in Canada to the local community groups that have shown interest in developing programs and business plans to take over the operation of airports throughout these communities.
Let me say at the outset that the comments I intend to make today are much the same as the comments I made when we went through committee and second reading in the House. We on this side agree in principle on the initiative of transferring the authority for the management of airports in Canada to local and community groups.
During the implementation of this program, though, we have some very vital concerns with respect to how this transfer of authority will take place, and those are the areas I wish to address today. I hope our colleagues on the other side of the House will take some interest in these remarks because it will mean a smooth and easy
June 3, 1991

transition from Department of Transport administration to that of local airport authorities.
What we will see here in the transition period is a similarity in Canada developing with what we already have seen in the United States where most of the airports are already operated by what is termed the local authority or a local management group. They have a far-reaching input into the affairs of airport management in their country, and we would hope it would be something analogous to what we will have here in Canada.
I cannot emphasize strongly enough that unlike the government's ill-conceived policy of deregulation in the transport industry the concept of local airport authority means better service to the communities we represent, and not less. Mainly for this reason we support in principle the idea and the thought of local airport authorities.
Local airport authorities are proceeding across Canada. Already, as we have heard, large communities are preparing to implement this policy. During the debate, as we crossed Canada on the Open Skies inquiry into getting better service between the United States and Canada, we heard very many vigorous approaches from people who had done a great deal to put themselves in place for the eventual taking over of the airports in their communities.
We were impressed with were the representations made by the airport authorities of the communities of Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver. I am told, but I am not sure at this stage, that there is an airport authority or steering group in the process of trying to bring local management in at Dorval airport.
It was interesting to hear these representations because the provincial governments in these three areas, Edmonton, Calgary, and Vancouver, were playing a very strong role in financing the local airports' initiatives. They are playing a strong role in fostering the idea that the area of responsibility should be at the local level.
Our cause for concern is simply-and I hope that this government would address this issue-the local airport authority act is dealing with every major airport in Canada and with smaller airports throughout the communities, but it is not addressing itself to the city of Toronto. One asks oneself: if local airport authorities are
Government Orders
good for the rest of Canada, why have we got a different plan for Lester B. Pearson Airport in Toronto?
Toronto is becoming the hub of Canada. It is not the hub of Ontario; it is the hub of Canada. This is the paradox and the dilemma we on this side find ourselves in. If government members are proposing local airport authorities, why are they not proposing the same administration for Lester B. Pearson Airport as they are for other regions in Canada? Why are they so intent on local airport authorities, with which we agree in principle, but not intent on establishing a local airport authority for Lester B. Pearson in Toronto?
As we know, the Lester B. Pearson Airport in Toronto has already proceeded on a mode of privatization. They have already privatized Terminal 3, Trillium Airport. They are in the process of asking for requests for the privatization of Terminal 2, which is the terminal Air Canada mainly uses. Since most of the international lines have moved out of Terminal 1, there is a refurbishing of that terminal and there will be a proposal to ask for its privatization.
Any of us who have travelled through Terminal 2 in the recent past since the refurbishing program has started know full well that Terminal 2 is becoming one of the fine airports not only in Canada but in North America. With limited resources-I think the spending estimates are somewhere around $57 million-they have done some magnificent work in Terminal 2. They have opened up the sides to let the people look at the aircraft and loading zones, improved the loading zones, increased the ability to walk that long corridor with raised stairways and stairwells and assisted the handicapped in that airport. It is much easier to use that facility now than what we have experienced in the past.
What I am saying is that an expenditure of $57 million is a lot of money. When we start talking about airports, $57 million does not go that far when we consider that Trillium cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $500 million to build.
What I am trying to say is: Why would we want to privatize a very functional airport such as Terminal 2 and lose control of those very important areas that bring some form of regulation back to the airline industry? I am talking particularly of the gates and the slots, the two most important elements in the administration of an airline carrier within an airport proper. We all know that at times when we land on an Air Canada flight at Pearson Airport, and we are waiting to get into a slot and a gate at Terminal 2, we can look over at Trillium,

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
Terminal 3, and find empty slots. The airline we may be using cannot get into that gate because it is not part of its system.
What I am saying is: Why should we be on a program to privatize Terminal 2 and take it out of public control or of local airport authorities whose main interest is supplying a good basis of airline traffic and control in the country?
I have nothing against private enterprise, but we know it has to pay $500 million or $600 million to recapture their investment in airline travel. I think the privatization concept, especially now with what Air Canada has done in Terminal 2, is something that I would wish and advise this government to reconsider. It should think of the consequences of totally privatizing the most important airport in Canada, while on the other hand we are asking to bring all other airports in Canada under local authority.
It is a paradox. It does not make sense. Why do we not just try to use one system throughout the country? The best system we see is a local airport authority. We on this side of the House think that Pearson International Airport with Terminals 1 and 2 should be considered for the local airport authority program-I see my colleague from Hamilton nodding her head-as well as what will happen under a local airport authority in Hamilton, to enhance the service to the travelling public.
I am sure this is not of prime consideration when privatization will cost upward of $1 billion for Terminals 1 and 2. We know that money, although the facilities at Terminals 1 and 2 are already very adequate, will just add to the cost to the air travelling public in Canada. It is something now that we should be looking at to try to defray the cost and keep the costs in line rather than let them expand.
I hope in the debate today as we discuss this bill that we get some response from our friends across to give us their idea of why on the one hand Terminals 1 and 2 in Toronto are not subject to the local airport authority as are all other airports in Canada.
As we talk about Pearson International Airport, we all know that the airlines in the United States have gone into what is called the hub and spoke operation, where they develop hubs throughout certain sections of the country. Then all the spokes of all the smaller airlines feed into this hub.
One of the unfortunate occurrences that we have seen in air travel in Canada is that when the hub does not operate the spoke cannot operate. If we continue to want to privatize Lester B. Pearson Airport in Tbronto and for some reason that hub does not work, it affects all air travel. All the spokes across this country coming into Toronto Pearson are then inoperative because of the events and the weather that could affect the operation of that main hub in the Canadian air system.
I often think of an analogy when we talk about hub and spoke. When we were kids we had bicycles, and the most important part of that bicycle was the rear hub. If that did not operate, you had tremendous problems. All the spokes that would lead out into this wheel would cause tire repairs. You just could not operate your bicycle.
When we take that analogy into consideration, if that hub at Lester B. Pearson is not going to be operative, the spokes are going to be inoperative. That is not good for the air travellers in Canada.
I would like to suggest-and I hope I get some comments from our friends on the other side in the interests of air travellers, air cargo, special services and all other incidental items that are involved in the vital transportation industry in Canada-that we retain some degree of control.
When I say "we", I mean Canadians through the ability of local airport authorities should maintain some degree of control through Terminals 1 and 2 in Tbronto. We could ensure that not only those who are using that facility but all other travellers from across Canada will have public input into the continued operation of that important hub at Lester B. Pearson Airport.
I would like to be parochial for a moment. In my own riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon, a committee has already been in place for well over 18 months and is preparing with great enthusiasm and great energy to meet the challenge of what local airports can bring and mean to our community.
June 3, 1991

The steering committee is a very competent group of people who have been gathered together and who welcome the chance to meet the needs of the community and run an airport authority in very cost efficient manner which because of bigness in our transportation system in this country leaves somewhat to be desired.
In establishing local airport authorities in general, efforts must be made to convince municipalities that this is not just another attempt by the government to divest itself of yet another financial burden. It was our concern in committee, it is our concern at second reading, and it is our concern today that as we transfer the authority to local airports we must ensure to every community in this country that the financial burden, if any, placed upon the operation of those airports will not result in the municipal taxpayer in every area of this country from being burdened with the operation of air services. That is not the intent. Members on this side of House would have nothing to do nor would we agree in any way with participating in this bill if it meant that the financial burdens of operating an airport would finally find their way into the local or municipal level. That is not the intent.
We on this side will always be on guard to make sure that the municipal taxpayer in Canada will not be forced or obligated to pay for air services in their own communities. It has always been a federal responsibility. It should continue to be a federal responsibility. What we are saying is that with the local airport authority we think and we trust that it will be an enterprise that can be self-paying.
Let me say, again with emphasis, that it is not our intention on this side of the House to place the financial burden of these airports on municipalities. It is an opportunity for municipalities to decentralize from Ottawa and other regional transportation offices so that the control of the airports themselves will become part of the local concern.
We must bear in mind that the intent of the legislation is to make airport management more responsive to the needs of any given community in Canada. At the same time it is imperative that Transport Canada remains responsible for all air side operations of the airport. Another cause of concern on this side of the House as we went through committee hearings was that an airport
Government Orders
has two components: it has an air side and it has a ground side.
The air side is not in any part negotiable in this agreement. The air side is responsible for the safety of air traffic in Canada, and I am talking about air traffic controllers and the training of air traffic controllers, their work schedules, the climate control and the atmospheric control. All those areas and all those government agencies are responsible for ensuring good, safe quality of air transportation in Canada. It is not part of this legislation and it shall remain intact for the safety of all air travellers in Canada.
We have a record in Canada with respect to air safety that is the envy of every country in the world. It is not our position on this side of the House that any of those safety features which respect air side be part of this. It should remain under the management and under the control of Transport Canada.
The ground side is the other aspect of air passenger services. Ground side operations, which is what we are referring to in this legislation, is the part we consider could be better administered by local airport authorities in the communities in which we reside.
It must be understood that the way in which a new system will operate is to afford the local authority the flexibility to manage according to local needs as far as the terminal and ground side facilities are concerned. As I said previously, ground side services only. The operation of the airport proper, the operation of the concessions, the operations of the grounds surrounding the runways and the use of those grounds to the best advantage of the community are all ground side services. Up to this point in time maybe the community has not had a fair chance to direct its best ability toward running that operation. That is where the local group will place its emphasis.
Consequently, given the sensible rationale approach to airport management, local authorities will be able to effect the changes the community needs, effect the changes the community deserves, and effect the changes on a very cost efficient basic.
I am speaking of improving services. When we talk of local airport authorities, I am speaking of improving the services these local airports already enjoying, not denying them any services; attracting more passengers to the air industry; attracting more industry that is responsive to the needs of the air industry; attracting more jobs

Government Orders
within the airport community than we heretofore have had; meeting all the needs of a region that an airport service requires; and operating these airports on a very cost effective basis.
Anyone should be able to see that these goals can best be met at the local level. I want to say at this time that in saying they can best be met at the local level, I am in no way insinuating or impugning any degree of not running these airports to the best of their ability by the present method of operation. They have done the best they can with the finances that they have had available to them and, as I say, the best they can not being part of the community. Being part of the community means they can offer better service.
As an example, if I can talk again about the community I represent and the airport, I think I can speak with a little authority on this because in one of my previous careers I spent several years working on airport property. There are several areas I have noticed that were perhaps not cost efficient and not properly administered mainly because of the absence of direct responsibility at that particular level.
Every major decision in the area that I represent was made 450-500 miles away from us. The decision affecting obligations in Ontario was made not in the province of Ontario but in another province. Perhaps these people who were making the decisions were not fully aware of the needs of Thunder Bay or north western Ontario; not only unaware of the needs, but these divisions operating under certain financial constraints which left the community, a smaller community like Thunder Bay, perhaps wanting because there were more important needs in other perhaps larger areas.
Let me perhaps give one example that I noticed when I was working at an airport. We are not talking a great deal of money. There was in the budgetary allotments for a period of time a request for security fencing around certain areas of the airport proper. I know this was on the expenditure side for several years and had been approved and taken out, approved and taken out. Then one day in the middle of winter, in fact it was toward the end of February, a construction firm moves into the local airport and starts to build the security fence around certain sections of the airport proper.
Building the fence is not an onerous job, but building a fence in the middle of February in Thunder Bay is not reasonable. We have a frost layer of approximately four feet. When they brought these huge machines in to dig holes to put the posts in, to dig through four feet of frost was next to impossible. The machines were there for about 30 days trying to get enough post holes dug through the frost layer in order to lay the fence.
After 30 days they gave up. They moved all of their equipment out of the community. To this day that fence has never been built. All I am saying is that if we had a proper airport authority on the site, first off we would not attempt to build a security fence and dig holes in the ground in the middle of February. We would do it on a more cost efficient basis and bring in contractors. Perhaps local contractors would be given the opportunity to come in and build that fence during the time it is conducive to do building of that type in the climate in which we live.
Another example that always caused me some concern in airports, not only in Thunder Bay but airports right across the country, was the methodology used in granting concessions on airport property.
I think we all know, those of us who live in smaller communities with airports, that the facilities provided at smaller airports are very, very important to the travelling public. During this period of time we have seen several concessions, especially the food concession, being administered and tendered out, and companies not from the community being involved in providing the service.
What eventually happens is that these companies find out that perhaps in smaller communities they do not have the volume of business they anticipated, that because of the fees charged for operating on airport property they are not doing as well as they expected. Then, several things happen: the service that is supposed to be provided starts to diminish, the facilities are not kept open during the time the travelling public requires those facilities, and the quality expected of an airport facility is not there. This is a trend that happens over a period of time.
What I have noticed is that when local concerns go into business enterprises at airports, they offer a good service and their reputation is involved. Just by way of example, the food service at the airport near where I live has had excellent service for the last 10 years, having taken over from a national company that could no longer provide the degree and the quality of service the people in our community expected. By bringing in a local
June 3, 1991

restaurateur to supply those services, we have had magnificent service in that airport for the last 10 years. I hope that in whatever expansion programs are going ahead in our area, he will be given an extra added responsibility to continue the fine service that he has provided over the years.
Those are just a couple of examples where local airport authorities can make a real contribution to the services that are needed by the travelling public in Canada.
While we on this side of the House affirm our support for the policy in principle, we are concerned that the aims of the policy do not meet the obligations in a very sensible and fair manner.
We on this side of the House feel that the objectives of local airport authorities should be three-fold. I am hoping that we will monitor, and I am sure we will monitor, the transfer of local airport authorities, considering that their primary objectives would be, first, to serve the local community interests, second, to enhance economic development and, third, to operate airports in a cost-effective manner.
When we talk about serving local community interests, we can look at different airports in this country that provide air services, usually Toronto because it is a hub. All of us have gone to smaller airports and have seen the competitive airlines leaving the airport basically at the same time, within 10 or 15 minutes of each other, both leaving at seven o'clock in the morning or 7.15 in the morning, both leaving for the same destination and both travelling with less than a full load-sometimes less than 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent of a load.
If we are really and truly interested in this country in cost saving and efficiency of fuel and in having our airports operate in an environment that allows them to produce a profit, perhaps the local airport authority could get involved in managing and assisting in the scheduling and providing of air services so that we would not see congestion at particular periods of time at airports, and then an absence of anybody at all waiting for the next aeroplane to arrive. This is clearly an area
Government Orders
where the authority, operating on a local level, can serve a community.
I should also mention that I am very proud of a facility which happens to be in our airport, and is there because of the great generosity of a local family. The facility is for a search and rescue group which covers all of northern Ontario and parts of northern Manitoba searching for missing aircraft. With the combination of the tremendous volunteer involvement of a friend of mine, John Illingworth, who was the instrument that provided the leadership in this area, and the contribution of this very fine family in providing an airport facility which they were not using at that time, we have been able to establish one of the finest search and rescue units in all of Canada. This is something we are very proud of.
That is the type of local initiative which is needed and perhaps will be increased as each airport in this country becomes governed by people with a local concern.
Let me address the enhancement of economic development. As we travel with the transport committee, and through our responsibilities as critics, visiting most airports in the country, one of the things that comes to mind very clearly is that airports are surrounded by huge tracts of land. What we see in this land that is available for development is an almost instant industrial site that has all the services-water and sewage, and fire treatment facilities-that every industrial site in this country requires. With each local authority which takes over in its community, we have immediately another industrial site available for the community to develop. On these industrial sites I would envisage all services of an industrial nature that are required to be in the approximate vicinity of the airport proper.
The cargo industry, which is developing and increasing throughout the country, indicates that cargo facilities would be very important additions to airport properties. The packaging business, getting packages from point A to point B overnight, should be on airport properties. If an airport serves a large regional community, storage areas for goods before they are transferred either to the job site, a mining site, a forestry site, or any other economic area that requires that service would be useful.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
These facilities are not now available at small airports throughout the country, but I am confident that if local authorities were to assess the needs of regional enterprise, they would begin to establish such facilities at all local airports.
This would also afford the opportunity to provide specialty services such as fire fighting, picture-taking facilities for designating areas for mining exploration, topography and cartography. Those facilities could be made available through the combined efforts of the authority and the local community.
Private recreational facilities which are growing by leaps and bounds in Canada can be further enhanced by local authorities in this country.
All of these ventures and initiatives taken by local authorities will enhance the cost-effectiveness of airports and perhaps create viable enterprise, the proceeds of which can be applied for the further benefit of the air-travelling public in Canada.
This legislation has only the bare bones of a policy which will become widespread throughout the country. It is so important that each community begins with good direction and guidance. Local airport management is in its infancy in Canada and this is a logical point to ensure that the policy gets off on the right foot, that mistakes are prevented, and that sound management principles are effected so that the community will benefit.
One of the very important considerations in this legislation is the fair treatment of personnel when authority is transferred from the Ministry of Transport to the local airport authority.
In my opinion, this bill does not go far enough in ensuring that Transport Canada employees will be totally protected during this transfer process.
I was surprised during the committee hearings, when we discussed this matter with the unions representing the employees working for Transport Canada, that there was no provision in their labour legislation that dealt with successor rights. Legislation like that should have a successor right provision in Canada, inasmuch as in the last four or five years we have seen a great change-over of Canadian ownership and businesses to private concerns. Without successor rights for the employees, it seems that there is some uncertainty with respect to
employees' benefit packages and all of the obligations for which Transport Canada is responsible that have been negotiated over the years.
Successor rights in labour legislation simply mean that if someone takes over the operation of a business, leases a business or by any other means starts to run an enterprise that up to that time has been run by someone else, then every union agreement that was entered into by the previous owner, lessor, or whatever the case may be must be maintained by the business enterprise taking over the venture.
Without that in the legislation, I can see why the employees in these areas across Canada would have some degree of concern.
Successor rights provisions provide for the same union representing the same employees from the previous employer to the future employer. It says in the successor rights provisions that during the transfer of ownership there will be no raiding of employees by another union. That is forbidden in the successor rights provisions.
These provisions guaranteed the veiy same terms of employment, working conditions, grievance procedures, wage package and benefits for employees under a local airport authority that they experienced while working for Transport Canada.
We are going to be looking very closely at the progress of this government program. Inasmuch as it is selling off many of the Canadian assets, during the transition period we are going to recommend to the government that successor rights be included as a very important addition to the legislation that governs federal employees in federal ministries.
In the transition of authority from the Minister of Transport and the Department of Transport to the local airport authorities, even if successor rights are not in the contract or in the labour legislation, all successor rights provisions under the Canada Labour Code should be adhered to.
In this government's headlong rush to deregulate, privatize and sell off every institution we have in Canada, individuals have the right to be protected. There is no better way to protect those rights than invoking the successor rights provisions we have in other labour legislation in this country.

Another crucial area that we are concerned about as we start to transfer authority is the matter of safety and security from federal standards in our airports to local airport authority standards.
I have already gone through the process of stating the differences between air and terminal security. On the air side, there will be a continuation. On the terminal side, there will be additions to the ground security areas and the baggage claiming areas. We hope that we will be able to implement through local airport authorities security measures ensuring that every piece of luggage be subject to an X-ray and not only carry-on luggage, and that the owner of that luggage is responsible to fly with it.
Those are some of the safety items we can implement through the local level that up until this point we have not been able to implement because of some divisions across the country with respect to how we analyse the luggage that goes on to our aircraft.
With respect to carry-on luggage, it is getting to be a terrible consideration in Canada because of the spoke and hub concept. We in smaller communities are not getting on to DC-9s or 727s or 747s anymore. We are getting on 30 passenger aircraft and 40 passenger aircraft which do not allow the passenger to carry on the amount of luggage as do the larger aircraft. We have to come to grips in Canada with this program of carry-on luggage, especially at small airports.
I am sure that local airport authorities can come to grips with this issue and implement procedures which will be beneficial to all Canadian travellers.
I can see that my time is up. If I had had more time, I would have liked to discuss some of the recommendations we had put forward, some of the changes we had hoped for in the previous bill.
Let me close with a proposed amendment to the bill before the House. I move, seconded by the member for Kingston and the Islands:
That the motion be amended by deleting the words "be now read a
third time and do pass" and by substituting therefor the following:
"be not read a third time, but be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport with instructions that the committee consider amending the bill in clause 2
(a) by striking out lines 21 and 22 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
