speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the intervention of the member from one of the Hamilton ridings. One only has to look at the full text of the speech to see the amount of time spent glowing over the concept to appreciate what was being said.
Let me come back to the point I was making, why I oppose local airport authorities. One of the obstacles in the way of an agreement between Canada and the United States in a new bilateral air arrangement is the fact that the federal government of the United States no longer has control over its airports. They have local airport authorities. They have state authorities. They have airports that are run by airlines.
The federal government of the United States cannot go in and implement a bilateral agreement without first having to seek the approval of each and every one of those local airport authorities. Their system is fragmented.
Second, my preference as a Canadian is to have a national system owned and operated by the people of Canada. This system has been in place for years, ever since C. D. Howe started Trans-Canada Airlines and set up the airports across this country. If we allow the airports to run their own show, then no one can be assured of consistency of service from one end of this country, from coast to coast to coast, because each airport authority will do its own thing.
Nor can we be assured, and certainly this bill does not speak to it, that each and every airport authority will be selected in the same manner. During the legislative committee meetings, and we heard from a number of the local airport authorities which are up and running and ready to use this act, we heard some excellent examples of how they selected their people. It was not a bunch of boys in the back room who got together and said: "Let's take over the local airport", but it was municipal chambers of commerce, municipal councils, who together developed a process for selecting the members of the local airport authority.
In the area around Montreal, individual members of council from the participating municipalities all sent representatives. Others draw from a cross-section of the community but they do it in a public way, unlike the city of Thunder Bay, where a group of individuals decided on
their own that they wanted to take over the local airport. There is no consistency and no protection for the public that have to use those facilities. That is where I am coming from in terms of the concept of local airport authorities.
Specifically, the purpose of the bill is to protect the collective bargaining rights, language rights and pension rights of federal public sector workers currently employed by Transport Canada during the transfer of airports from Transport Canada to local airport authorities. While we agree with the principle that the workers must be protected, we do not believe that this bill really does that. Certainly there is a lack of clarity in the bill, and in light of current worker-management relations, it does not provide the protection it purports to provide.
The union representing the workers, the Union of Transport Canada Employees, has cited several problems with this bill. Let me be specific. Workers or their representatives have not been a part of the process of negotiation and consultation that has gone on between Transport Canada and various local airport authorities. They are being presented with a take it or leave it option. This is not a good basis upon which to build good worker-employer relations. Second, the procedural and substantive rights of workers with regard to their existing pensions under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act are not clear under this bill. It is being left up to Treasury Board to make regulations. Again, there has been no consultation on the development of these regulations with the workers involved.
Most importantly, the bill contemplates removing the workers from these plans. In the case of other privatizations of work places, workers have remained in these plans. This bill needs to incorporate the desires of workers to continue under these plans because it should be noted that the local airport authority in British Columbia is having difficulty finding an insurance company to take on the disability insurance plan currently provided workers. They have been told that it would be too expensive to continue this type of coverage. What are they to do? Third, the continuation of the bargaining agent is also a matter of great concern. The bill provides for the continuation of the terms and conditions of an existing collective agreement at the time of transfer. However, past experience with other privatizations is that the determination of the appropriate bargaining
June 3, 1991

agent is a very long and disruptive process. This bill should incorporate provisions so that the existing bargaining agent remains in place for the period of one full collective agreement after the transfer in order to ensure the protection of workers' rights and the orderly determination of a bargaining agent.
The bill also fails in clause 4 to make clear that all services to the travelling public will continue to be provided in both official languages. Let me repeat that. The bill fails, in clause 4, to make clear that all services to the travelling public will continue to be provided in both official languages. We need to see in this bill provisions ensuring that third parties under contract to the local airport authority be required to provide their services under the linguistic terms currently set out in the Official Languages Act and any regulations made under that act.
The exclusion of those parts of the Official Languages Act dealing with services to the public and language of work are a serious undermining of the quasi-constitutional status of the Official Languages Act. According to the Official Languages Commissioner, any dismemberment of quasi-constitutional legislation can only be perceived as an erosion that is incompatible with the importance of its guarantees to Canada and Canadians. The commissioner recommended that all provisions of the Official Languages Act be incorporated by the local airport authorities.
That is something we attempted to do in committee. Both myself and the Liberal transport critic had identical motions which would have put back into the act certain sections, including Part V of the Official Languages Act, that would have provided protection for both language groups the ability to work in the language of their choice, the requirement to serve their customers in the language of the customer's choice.
The government said no. It said no to the English speaking minority in Montreal. It said no to the French speaking minority of Ottawa or any other community outside of Quebec that has a reasonably sized French speaking population. But the government has failed to
Government Orders
protect the minority rights of the English speaking workers at the Montreal airport.
We made an attempt to change that. The two Liberal members on the committee, the critic, the associate critic, the member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and I all voted to put that clause back into the act. One of the amendments I had wanted to have debated today and would have argued to you that even though it had been defeated in committee it was of paramount importance for the matter to be seized again and debated here in this House.
Perhaps there will still be an opportunity should we, through our House leaders, reach some kind of agreement to revert to report stage at a later part today.
I want to say it is a fundamental issue that if we are going to take a federal service, a federal airport and turn it over to a local airport authority, then along with that transfer should be the transfer of obligations under the Official Languages Act. We should not have two different classes of airports in this country. What is next? Our train stations or perhaps, part of the House of Commons. Maybe we will have an English speaking wing, or a French speaking wing and we carve them out.
No, Mr. Speaker. I think the government has made a fundamental error in this particular bill, in the need to provide legislative protection for workers, at what will still be federal airports. They will have a local management, but they will still be federal airports and there is no reason on earth that I can find, that is acceptable to me, why they should be exempted.
This bill may not be the privatization of airports, but it is the privatization of the workplace. The government has a responsibility to ensure the rights of its workers are protected before, during and after the transfer. This bill gives only more uncertainty. If the purpose is to stabilize worker-management relations, then the workers must be consulted and their concerns heeded before this legislation is implemented. Given this government's current disdain for its own workers, how can it be trusted to act in their best interests when negotiating with local airport authorities? Clear legislation is needed, setting out the obligations of the government, the obligations of the local airport authority and the rights of workers.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
Other instances of privatizing the workplace, for example, security services at airports, have been of questionable benefit. Let us not forget that one of the airports we are talking about devolving to a local airport authority is the Edmonton International Airport, which has just come through a strike by their security guards searching for a decent contract. What did this airport do? They laid off the workers while they were on strike. Is that the kind of labour-management relations we expect to see, by passing this kind of legislation and this kind of privatization of the workplace?
There have been ongoing discussions between the minister and his staff and my caucus colleague, the critic for labour, who has been handling this bill. There were some agreements. There was some willingness on the part of the government to, in fact, accept a provision for retroactive payment for employees who have left the Public Service.
In fact, the former Minister of Transport, Mr. Lewis, wrote back, as follows, with a suggested amendment.
That Bill C-85 be amended by adding, immediately after line 26 on page 5, the following:
8. Where the Minister has sold, leased or otherwise transferred an airport to a designated airport authority and, after the transfer date, a collective agreement or arbitral award under the Public Service Staff Relations Act provides for a retroactive increase in remuneration to a day before that date for employees in a bargaining unit in which designated employees for the airport were employed immediately before that date, the provisions of the collective agreement or arbitral award respecting retroactive increases in remuneration shall apply to those designated employees in respect of the retroactive period before that date.
The former minister was prepared to see this particular change made in the legislation. I understand that the government has other items it needs to incorporate into this legislation to ensure that this bill is workable, matters relating to taxation for one.
I would encourage the government to give serious consideration to reopening this bill today for clause by clause review at report stage. Both the Liberals and myself have given the Table the amendments so it will
have had an opportunity to review them if this House decides, through unanimous consent, to revert.
I would like to spend the last couple of minutes going back over the philosophy of devolving to local airport authorities. It is not in the best interests of Canadians. There is a carrot out there that these local airport authorities believe, and I do not doubt their belief, that they can manage that building and those grounds in a way that is different from the way the local airport manager, under the policies of Transport Canada, can do.
I would suggest that if there are problems with the policies of Transport Canada, let us change those policies to provide the local manager with much more flexibility to use the capital funds available to enhance the operation, but let us not fool ourselves. In a lot of cases any wealth that is created at an airport will not necessarily be new wealth. It might be redirected wealth.
For example, in the city of Thunder Bay the proposal there, as I understand it, is that they are looking at more retail opportunities within the airport itself. Is that going to take away retail opportunities in the downtown core? Is that just going to rob Peter to pay Paul, with none of us really benefiting? If it is just aimed at the travelling public, then perhaps it might work from that point of view.
Will they be in competition with the city of Thunder Bay in terms of industrial land? Will they be taking needed revenue away from some of our light industrial areas and having them located at the airport and not contribute in the same way? We have to be careful that when we embrace these concepts we fully understand the impact on our communities.
Are people going to be happy finding different levels of services from airport to airport to airport? Some would say that is the case today and I would agree. However I think in the case of the Thunder Bay airport, which incidentally is in my riding of Thunder Bay-Ati-kokan, we work very closely with Transport Canada-we being the municipal politicians, myself, the Chamber of Commerce-to bring about improvements. We have a program under way this summer to do a temporary upgrade in the building.
June 3, 1991

We have on stream, on track, on time a major replacement of the airport terminal building, in time for the 1995 World Nordic Games, a commitment made by the former Minister of Transport to the people of Thunder Bay. We did not need a local airport authority to do that. We just needed a willingness to work toward an end.
One of the ironies is that the group that now wants to be this local airport authority were the backers of the previous government who made promise after promise after promise for a new terminal or for expansion that they never carried through with.
I know I have a few seconds left. I urge the government to reconsider the concept not to go forward with the devolution of airports to local airport authorities, but to enhance the operations, enhance the flexibility of the airport managers, some whom I have met. They are excellent representatives of the Crown and do a fantastic job, whether it is Thunder Bay, Toronto or elsewhere, in providing services to people because that is what it is all about.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am intervening in this debate because this bill has serious implications for our official language policy in Canada. When our airports were owned and operated by the Government of Canada, they were fully subject to the provisions of the Official Languages Act.
That meant that all our airports under the ownership and control of the government had to respect the two official languages in Canada, had to provide services in the two official languages of Canada and had to respect employees who worked in those airports who were of one or the other official languages.
With this bill and the privatization of certain of our airports, the government is allowing these privatized airports to escape certain provisions of the Official Languages Act. For example, under the bill only Parts IV, VIII, IX and X of the Official Languages Act, 1988, will apply to privatized airports but not Parts V, VI and VII.
When Air Canada was privatized by this government a short while ago, the bill was changed or amended so that all provisions of the Official Languages Act would apply to the privatized Air Canada. So there seem to be some anomalies here. While the government agreed to the
Government Orders
application of all provisions of the Official Languages Act to Air Canada for some reason or other, it is hesitant to go that distance in this bill dealing with the privatization of airports.
We are in a debate and we are hopeful that the arguments of opposition members and some others, one would hope some others on the government side, would convince the government that it should do the same for airports as it did for Air Canada.
The Commissioner of Official Languages, whose job it is to look out for the language rights of minorities in this country, appeared before the appropriate committee in the last session of Parliament when this bill's predecessor was going through the various stages. The Commissioner of Official Languages objected to those provisions in this bill which exempted the privatized airports from various sections of the Official Languages Act.
The commissioner said: "I therefore strongly recommend to the committee that section 4 of Bill C-85" which was what it was called at that time, "be amended to ensure that, as in the case of the decisions taken in the privatization of Air Canada, all the provisions of the Official Languages Act continue to apply to the designated airport authorities. Any weakening of this policy would seem to us to be unacceptable and an unjustified step backwards."
That is what was said by the Commissioner of Official Languages.
He was even concerned about those clauses that pretend to give service to the public in both official languages. He said, with respect to section 4: "I refer here to services provided by third parties under contract, specifically the various tenants and concessionaires in airport terminals concerning whom we have received more than 200 complaints in the past three years." He goes on to say that this section 4(2) is ambiguous and it does not clearly set out that service to the public must be provided, not only by the airport authorities, but by the concessionaires operating in those airports.
He said: "I therefore strongly recommend that the wording of subsection 4(2) be revised to ensure that third parties under contract are required to provide their services under the linguistic terms currently required by the Official Languages Act and the regulations made under it."

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
That is what was said by the Commissioner of Official Languages.
Strange as it may seem, those who manage the Montreal International Airport have approached myself and other members of Parliament objecting to the application of all the provisions of the Official Languages Act to the Montreal International Airport. The reasons given by the authorities in Montreal are that if the Montreal airport and other airports that are privatized must comply with all the provisions of the Official Languages Act, they will not be competitive with the airports in Boston and New York, or Terminal 3 in Toronto.
Let me deal first with Boston and New York. Of course the American airports have not provided bilingual services in English and French for any period of their history, as far as I know. However, that has not prevented us in Canada from providing services in both those languages because we have populations which speak those two languages. We have pilots who speak those two languages. We have employees working in the airport who speak those two languages. We have always thought, and so did the Conservative government in 1988 when it passed the new Official Languages act, that services to the public should be provided in two official languages.
It also thought that in federal institutions there should be equitable participation by both official language groups and that there should be fairness and justice with respect to the employees and their language of work in both official languages.
I find the argument of the authorities in Montreal rather strange because I was in this Parliament a few years ago when there was an attempt to make sure that air traffic control services in this country be in the two official languages. That received strong support from Montreal.
The people there who were air traffic controllers whose mother tongue was French and pilots who were French-speaking felt that air traffic control in this country should be in two official languages. We fought for that and put it into effect.
Despite the fears that were raised by certain opponents at the time, we have had bilingual air traffic
control in several airports for many years now, and there has been no danger or great concern. It has worked very well.
Consequently, therefore, I cannot see why we, in order to compete with Boston and New York, should lessen our commitment to official languages. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that if Montreal was to operate totally in the two official languages, it would be more competitive because it would attract travellers, workers and employees who were competent in both languages. However, in Boston you are not assured that they can speak your language at all.
This is something that has to be examined more closely. For this reason, I am pleased that my colleague from Thunder Bay moved that this bill go back to committee so we can examine some of these issues.
I am not convinced that applying the provisions of the Official Languages Act, as we have for years to all our airports, will hurt our competitiveness with the airports in Boston and New York.
With respect to Terminal 3, the manager of the Montreal airport says this would also make the Montreal airport non-competitive with respect to Terminal 3 which he says is not subject to all the provisions of the Official Languages Act.
Terminal 3, which is a new terminal and was only opened recently, was built as a privatized airport from the beginning. It was never under government authority as were the other airports and it was built on a contract with a certain private firm. It is principally served by Canadian Airlines International.
I have looked at the contract between the Government of Canada and the Terminal 3 developers. It seems to me from reading the contract that Terminal 3 is subject to the Official Languages Act, but this requires some serious legal analysis.
This is another reason for this bill to go back to committee. If the government in the contract with the Terminal 3 developers did relax the provisions of the Official Languages Act with respect to airports even before this bill was passed, then I would say the government is speaking with a forked tongue.
On one hand, it is supporting an official languages policy such as it set out in the Official Languages Act of 1988 and on the other hand, it is already privatizing or
June 3, 1991

setting up privatized airports which do not respect all the provisions of that law.
Either the Official Languages Act of 1988 means something or it means nothing. When the government put that bill before Parliament in the early months of 1988, the Prime Minister stood in his place and said that this policy was so important for Canada that if he had his way, Parliament would sit all night in order to have it passed.
We did pass the bill. It was passed with the support of the Liberal and the New Democratic Party opposition but the opposition came not from the opposition parties but from certain members of the government's own party who, at that time, were known as the dinosaurs. They sort of opposed the bill, held it up and so on, but the opposition did not come from the opposition parties.
Despite the words of the Prime Minister in 1988 when the bill was passed that it was so important to pass that revised bill on official languages, we still do not have the regulations for that bill. It is more than two years since the bill was passed. The government has presented to committee the draft regulations with respect to service to the public, but it has not yet presented the regulations which are required for the language of work or equitable participation or promotion or advancement of the official languages in Canada. One wonders about the commitment of the government to official languages.
The reason for the Official Languages Act and for an official languages policy is that we have in this country large numbers of people who speak both official languages. About one-third of the population of the country is French speaking. The other two-thirds are English speaking but come from many backgrounds.
There are some who would suggest that all of Quebec should perhaps be French speaking: we would allow those airports and those institutions to be unilingual French and in the other nine provinces everything would more or less operate in English.
That sort of suggestion forgets that there are almost one million Canadians who speak French, living outside the province of Quebec. Almost one million francophone Canadians are living outside Quebec who speak
Government Orders
French and want to be served in their language and want to work in their language, where they are in sufficient numbers.
We are not talking about one employee in Vancouver in some particular office. We are talking about large numbers of employees and particularly when they are dealing with the travelling public. Very often businessmen from Montreal go to Winnipeg for conferences. They go to Halifax to deal with governmental matters and so on. That is the nature of our country.
When the government introduced and passed the Official Languages Act in 1988 it was committed to that policy. It was a good law. It had to be completed by regulations, but it was a good law. Now we are bit concerned that the government is backing off from that.
We say that this bill is defective in that it does not apply all the provisions of the Official Languages Act to the airports the government is attempting to privatize under this bill. We are asking the question: Why is it members of the government agreed to apply all the sections of the Official Languages Act to Air Canada when they privatized Air Canada, and rightly so? They should have done that. As I said, Air Canada is our major airline and it is dealing with the travelling public, both English and French speaking Canadians. If Air Canada is to follow all the provisions of the Official Languages Act, surely the airports where these Air Canada planes land, take off and work should also follow all the provisions of the Official Languages Act.
I fully support the amendment presented by my colleague from Thunder Bay, that this bill be sent back to committee where we can once again examine certain provisions, certain sections of it, and especially those sections that relate to official languages.

The hon. member for Edmonton East, and then the hon. member for Hamilton West.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, might I preface my remarks on the bill and the amendment by noting, for the benefit of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, that our caucus is in fact composed of 44 members, not 42. There may be two who you would wish expelled, but that is not yet the case.
I would like in rising to speak on the amendment, and of course therefore on the bill as well, to note that I think there is considerable merit in the amendment. When the vote comes it is my intention to vote for it, as I believe is the case for all members of the caucus of which I am a member.
I cannot be quite so charitable in the instance of the bill itself. There are flaws with the bill, especially given that, ostensibly at least, the purpose of the bill is to protect the collective bargaining rights, the language rights, the pension rights-the workers' rights-of federal public sector workers currently employed by Transport Canada during the transfer of airports from the authority of Transport Canada to the so-called local airport authorities, the LAAs.
There are elements in this bill which make it very unlikely that that goal will be properly and fully effected. I would like to deal just briefly with two of those elements.
The first has to do with, generally, the rights of workers at what are now federal government airports. I should note that given this government's current disdain for its own workers, it is somewhat problematic that we accept the assertion that it can be trusted to act in their best interests when negotiating with local airport authorities. Clear legislation is needed setting out the obligations of the government, the obligations of the local airport authorities and the rights of the workers employed by either or both.
This was brought home forcefully to me in the past six months in consequence of the situation faced by the passenger screening guards at the Edmonton International Airport. The service provided by these guards was contracted out quite some significant time ago.
Whereas at one time they were like all other employees at the Edmonton International Airport, employees of Transport Canada, in consequence of the government's ongoing program of contracting out, deregulation and privatization-you know the litany, Mr. June 3, 1991

Speaker-they ceased being Transport Canada employees some time ago. They remained, for the time being, members of the Union of Canadian Transport Employees, that union which represented them when they were Transport Canada employees. However, other than that, their formal ties as employees of Transport Canada were severed and they became employees of another company.
The company at the time was Canadian Protection Services. The contractual arrangement was one that saw Air Canada, as the lead airline using the Edmonton International Airport, contract for passenger screening, which is to say security services, with the private sector company, Canadian Protection Services. This was, I suppose, to start at least an agreeable contract for the signing parties, they being Air Canada on behalf of all airlines using the airport and Canadian Protection Services.
It was most clearly not terribly acceptable to the passenger screening guards, 66 of whom were employed at the airport by Canadian Protection Services, that is CPS, and all of whom were most desirous of improving the conditions of their work and the wages for which they worked.
Bargaining with CPS for a first collective agreement began in the spring of 1990, more than a year ago. At that time the union, the Union of Canadian Transport Employees, wished to have addressed several questions including the annual 200 per cent turnover rate among the employees retained as passenger screening guards by CPS at the Edmonton International Airport.
Number two was the fact that these employees were the only ones in the entire airport required to pay for their own parking, at a rate of $20 a month. Another was they were required to place $150 deposit on their uniforms. Of course, of key importance were the seriously low rates of pay. The union had hoped to raise the current levels of pay in the $6 to $6.49 an hour range to about $8 an hour, hardly a princely sum.
Unfortunately no agreement with CPS was reached. In November of last year the parties went to conciliation. This too proved fruitless. This left the employees in a no-win situation. They could strike but, if they struck, that would immediately create a situation in which their employer, CPS, was in violation of its contract with Air Canada. That being the case, the provision in that contract that allowed Air Canada then to cancel it would kick in, or they could simply knuckle under, as indeed
Government Orders
CPS had to knuckle under, because CPS was not getting the money from Air Canada and the other airlines using the airport to pay the passenger screening guards a reasonable amount. In that sense, CPS too was also locked into a no-win situation.
The predictable happened. In March of this year the 66 passenger screening guards went on strike. After two weeks, Air Canada determined that in consequence of the strike CPS was no longer able to live up to its contract to supply passenger screening services at the airport and, accordingly, Air Canada cancelled that contract. This meant, of course, that in the twinkling of an eye those 66 passenger screening guards were not on strike; they were unemployed.
Air Canada quickly reached an agreement with another security company, Aeroguard, which itself is a union company.
Its employees are represented by the United Food and Commercial Workers. This company, Aeroguard, resumed passenger screening services at the airport.
Many of the 66 passenger screening guards who had previously worked for CPS in that capacity at the airport now signed on with Aeroguard. Several did not.
The point here is that in the context of a contracted out privatized service, the protections of the Canada Labour Act which otherwise would have been completely available for those passenger screening guards were not there.
They were treated with contempt by Air Canada and the other contracting airlines at that airport. There is nothing that they or anyone else could do about it.
I wrote two letters, on March 7 and on March 21, to the then Minister of Transport, now the Solicitor General. I noted in the second:
For exercising Iheir right to strike, these 66 workers have now lost their jobs. This is grotesquely unfair. If, as ought to be the case, these workers were employed by Transport Canada and thus afforded the coverage of the Canada Labour Code directly, such jack-boot union busting, strike breaking would be illegal. And that's as it should be.
I received a reply from the current Minister of Transport dated May 13 of this year. He writes in part: "Security screening guards are employed by private industry." True. "They are not contracted to or through the federal government and cannot be considered as contracted out employees." True. "Nor, in this instance,

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
are they employed for the purpose of government agencies." True.
"Security guards are, like many Canadians, performing important jobs as employees of private industry in accordance with government regulations." Again, true.
"I must stress that they are not in any way denied rights or benefits to which they are entitled as a result of their status." Absolutely true, and that is precisely the problem. Their status is such that they are now denied the coverage of the Canada Labour Code.
I greatly fear that in the legislation we have before us today, we are setting the stage for hosts of other federal employees now employed at Canada's airports to join these unhappy passenger screening guards in that nonstatus situation.
For that reason, I find the bill inadequate. I would hope that when the amendment of the hon. member is passed by this House, as I hope, and the bill is therefore referred back to committee, these matters too will be addressed in committee at that time.
I say "these matters" because there is a second matter I would like to raise. It has to do with official languages.
I have, on numerous occasions in my home riding of Edmonton East and around Alberta, defended the Official Languages Act. I have defended the French language in Alberta. I have especially defended its general use in federal institutions in Alberta.
I believe that every Canadian has the right to deal with her or his federal government in the official language of their choice, regardless of where they are in this country. I will not abandon that position. I will continue to defend it in Edmonton, in Alberta and everywhere else in Canada where I can be allowed the privilege of raising my voice.
It is in this instance that I note with some dismay that portion of the bill which would exempt from the operations of the Official Languages Act the LAA airport in Montreal.
The bill would specifically omit that airport from the operations of Part V and Part VI of the Official Languages Act which provides, among other things, in Section 34 that:
English and French are the languages of work in all federal institutions, and officers and employees of all federal institutions have the right to use either official language in accordance with this Part.
Which in section 36(2) reads:
Every federal institution has the duty to ensure that, within the National Capital Region and in any part or region of Canada, or any place outside Canada, that is prescribed for the purpose of paragraph 35(l)(a), such measures are taken-to establish and maintain work environments of the institution that are conducive to the effective use of both official languages and accommodate the use of either official language by its officers and employees.
The effects of one of the main elements in this bill will be to remove that protection from the workers at the Montreal airport. This means that there is nothing to prevent the emergence at the Montreal airport, or at least those Montreal airports operated by what will be its local airport authority, of a strictly francophone language regime.
That is bad for two reasons. It is bad for the employees who work there, who require English as their first language to do their work. However, in some cases, more importantly, it is bad for the anglophone language minority in Montreal which may depend on the provision of anglophone services at its airports for their use of those airports. Again, this is not unreasonable. It is a keystone element of the Canadian Confederation that any citizen of this country may be able to deal with her or his government and its agencies and institutions in the official language of their choice.
To the degree that this bill detracts from that fundamental Canadian right, indeed detracts from that constitutional provision, the bill is flawed. Therefore, it is a second reason why I cannot, in conscience, fully and enthusiastically endorse this bill as it now stands.
Therefore, I would recommend to all members of this House, in the interest of equity and in the interest of prudence and, to hearken back to my first point, most of all in the interest of fairness for the workers at these airports, that this bill be referred back to the committee and that the hon. member's amendment be adopted.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to have the opportunity to rise on third reading debate of Bill C-15, the Airport Transfer Act, which was Bill C-85 in its previous incarnation before the government decided to prorogue, a government action which we, on this side of the House and
June 3, 1991

probably most Canadians, are still puzzled about and are asking ourselves why.
The bill concentrates on some technical matters related to the transference of what are currently Transport Canada operated facilities and will become local airport authorities under negotiations with Transport Canada. There are currently four major airports entering final negotiations with the federal government. They are Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton and Montreal.
There are a number of other airports which are interested in becoming local authorities. This means that the control and direction of the facilities will be shared at the local level between business, local officials and public representation.
Bill C-15 falls short, however, in attempting to deal with the maintenance of certain aspects of the day-today operation of federally regulated institutions-namely the official language protection for services and workers, job security, pension benefits and labour relations. It is enough to send shivers down anyone's spine.
On the first point, I support the comments made by my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, that the protection for both official languages in terms of services provided to the public and for job opportunities is, at best, weak. I am surprised that this government, which attempted to put a new face on the Official Languages Act, should now weaken its support with this bill.
The point is that the responsibility for these airports is federal until such time as it should be contracted away. All aspects pertaining to the Official Languages Act with respect to certain services are protected and should remain so once the facilities transfer over to local control.
In the case of Air Canada, for example, I am sure most Canadians would recognize the duality of Air Canada in its operations. It has a bilingual staff and there is equal opportunity for both language groups to advance within the corporation.
Once Air Canada was sold off, the government ensured that all aspects of the Official Languages Act remained intact.
Government Orders
In the case of these federally regulated facilities, regulated by the Canadian government, the same protection must apply. Services must be offered to all travelling Canadians in both official languages. In the same spirit, equal opportunity to both languages groups must be granted in hiring and advancement policies.
The second point of the bill essentially deals with labour relations. The bill as it stands does not satisfy this side of the House. At committee stage we tried to move several amendments which we thought would improve the bill, but were of course voted down by the Conservative majority on the committee.
Under this bill, job security for airport employees is not guaranteed. Airport managers will have full control over the work force of the airport and if management were to decide that 20 employees should be laid off to meet costs, a six month notice is all that would be required. That is shameful. Perhaps that may appear to be generous by others on the other side of this House, but the point is that it will severely undermine the collective bargaining process.
Airport employees at Transport Canada facilities have worked long and hard for their rights, which include job protection, among other things, and they should be protected under this privatization drive by the government and not sacrificed.
I heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport declare just this veiy morning that one of the blessings of this bill is that it will allow the local authorities to function on a non-profit basis. What that means is that yes, 20 or so employees who have worked for years to obtain their rights may be laid off in six months in order to meet costs, but the facilities must be self-supporting and the authorities will have to do what they must to operate on a non-profit basis.
An important point which I would like to take note of in relation to the non-profit basis of these authorities is that our party strongly opposes local taxes in municipalities considering these transfers being raised in order to finance the debt load of a local airport authority.
At this point I would also like to clarify a point that was made a little earlier in this debate with regard to Hamilton airport. Hamilton, interestingly enough, has witnessed a move not to a local airport authority but it is the creation of a regional airport management board. That is a wonderful blend of the private sector and government accountability. It is not becoming an independent authority. It still has the arrangement of a lease

Government Orders
agreement between the management group at Hamilton airport and Transport Canada.
The regional airport management board at Hamilton is now in the process of selecting five community representatives. Six members of that management board will be selected from the regional council. There is that wonderful blend between business and what it has to offer and the government accountability.
We in Hamilton have to be cognizant of, and this relates back to taxes, the fact that Hamilton airport does receive $700,000 in subsidy money from the federal government every year. If we decided to move to a local airport authority, where is $700,000 going to originate from? We can guess that it will be saddled right back with the taxpayer.
I mentioned in this House last week that Transport Canada lacks a master plan for air traffic in southern Ontario. It also lacks a master plan for the entire country's air traffic system which consists of our airports.
While the government negotiates a variety of contracts with various Canadian cities in order for them to move to local airport authorities, there are a host of other airports which will remain in the hands of Transport Canada.
Communication is essential for the over all system to work. The lack of an over all vision in transportation has created what I like to refer to as a helter-skelter approach to air transportation in this country.
Just this very morning I drove to Pearson International Airport and boarded the Air Canada flight at seven o'clock and picked up the local Toronto newspaper. In the editorial was an example of why there should be some kind of an over all vision for transportation in this country.
We on this side of the House are appalled by the inconsistency of government action. Here in part is what the editorial had to say.
"It all began when Ottawa gave Terminal 3's private owners 'sole and absolute discretion' over cab licences at the new facility where-" -as we are all familiar-"one
airline promises travellers 'the Dawn of Civilized Air Travel.' "
"Realizing its error in creating two different taxi systems at Canada's biggest airport, Ottawa bought back the licence rights for an undisclosed amount. To recoup its loss, the government hiked annual fees for Pearson taxis to $4,250 from $1,000; limo rates have gone to $6,000 from $1,000."
The ministers office still regards the payment to Terminal 3's owners as some kind of a state secret. We find that quite incredible. This piecemeal approach does little to address many issues of-you can put it under this title-"protection". We are talking about protection for the safety and security of the air travelling public. We are talking about protection for existing employees at our airports, protection for the physically challenged, protection of the Official Languages Act and protection against local taxes being increased to finance the debt load of a local authority.
These conditions can and would be addressed if, as so eloquently enunciated by my colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon, we consider his amendments to Bill C-15, put forward in this House, such as the amendment to return this debate to a committee where we can address these outstanding issues. These issues are of a vital concern, not only to this party, but to the New Democratic Party. It will stand today and say: "Yes, we oppose this legislation." What it is not saying is that this is an idea that can be flushed out and it can be done in a non-partisan way in a committee where it belongs. Let us take it back to committee, have another look at it, bring it back to the House and let us accomplish something here today.
Today we have established many reasons and conditions for the granting of our support to this bill. Especially, we focus and highlight official languages and job security. Those two are paramount.
I cannot understand why this government would transfer airports without justly guaranteeing full job security and fully protecting the linguistic rights of the employees at different airports in this country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to Statements by Members, pursuant to Standing Order 31.
June 3, 1991

Mr. Speaker, this week will be our twentieth National Environment Week, in as many years. Why not decide this week to act now?
1 want to invite all municipalities in my riding and all my constituents to take an active part in National Environment Week. Plant a tree, sow flower seeds, hang flower pots from your balcony, clean up the yard, tune up your car's engine and especially, Mr. Speaker, think in terms of recycling and reducing the quantity of garbage we produce: those are a few of the things we can do to help the environment.
Mr. Speaker, cleaning up our environment is good for us and our quality of life, but it is even better for future generations to whom we want to leave a healthier environment and a better world.

Mr. Speaker, as we begin Environment Week, Canadians across the country are questioning this government's commitment to a sustainable future.
Canadians are thinking globally and acting locally to protect our planet and are yearning for leadership from government.
Sadly, it is all too clear that the green plan is a whitewash and that no leadership is forthcoming from this government.
This past weekend, I proposed the creation of a biosphere reserve in the Gulf Islands of my constituency as a positive step toward preserving this pristine region and as a tool for economic development. This proposal meets community concerns, will prevent the further erosion of a delicate ecosystem and will lead to economic growth.
I challenge the government to show that it means what it says, to act to protect unique and threatened areas of Canada's coast, to establish a Gulf Islands' biosphere reserve for the benefit and interest of all Canadians.
I challenge the minister and this government to take some initiative, learn from the environmental activists they applaud and to act to fast-track environmental concerns for a change.
My constituents want to see jobs and a better environment. Now is the time for action.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a society composed of people from many different ethnic, regional, linguistic, religious and racial backgrounds. It is a nation whose very identity is defined by its diversity. Canada must not forget that the debate on national unity is not only one between English and French nor only one between Quebec and the rest of Canada, but is one for all Canadians. It is a quest for a national identity that includes Canadians of all backgrounds.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, we can only build a strong united country if we do it together, a country that acknowledges that every person, whatever his ethnic origin, race or sex, is entitled to a good quality of life.

Mr. Speaker, the throne speech made reference to changes the government is considering to give more independence and freedom to members of Parliament.
While this is being planned, I would like to let the government know what changes the member for Halton-Peel would like to see. The member would like to have more free votes in the House of Commons so the views of his constituents could be well represented. The member would like to have parliamentary committees empowered so that the government is under some obligation to act on all-party committee reports and recommendations.

June 3, 1991
The member for Halton-Peel would like to see more checks and balances with respect to cabinet appointments. They should be reviewed by members of Parliament sitting on committees. This member wants parliamentary reform with new mechanisms for public involvement and participation. This member never again wants his vote in the House of Commons wiped out, annulled by the vote of unelected and unaccountable senators.
The people want change. The government has indicated it is ready to listen and act. Freer MPs, Mr. Speaker, will make for freer Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as soon as the new gun control bill was tabled in Parliament, the gun lobbies started their usual propaganda that the new bill will not reduce violent crime, but only interfere with legitimate gun owners.
This is total nonsense and it is the nonsense that has been repeated by the gun lobby every time we attempt to tighten our gun laws. As a matter of fact, each time we tightened our gun laws, the rate of crime with guns declined. Countries with stricter gun control have lower rates of crime with guns. In the United States, 70 per cent of homicides are committed with guns.
In Canada, due to stricter laws, only 30 per cent of homicides are committed with guns.
In the United States, the homicide rate is 10 per 100,000; in Canada, it is 2.2 per 100,000. While this bill on gun control is not perfect, there is no doubt that it will make it more difficult for irresponsible and dangerous persons to obtain and use guns.
This bill should be supported and, if possible, strengthened.

Mr. Speaker, after statements by some federal members of the Liberal party
and members of the Bloc quebecois, especially those from large urban areas who know nothing about regional development programs in Quebec's resource regions, I have a few comments to make.
Today, these opposition members are upset by the federal government's decision and especially by the effective work being done by the minister and member for Roberval, the hon. Benoit Bouchard, They should read the article by Gilles Normand, published in La Presse on May 31. Mr. Bouchard simply implemented an administrative change which does not in any way affect funding procedures, but will make it easier for companies to have access to the program, and Quebecers will benefit, all of which will be done in co-operation with the Government of Quebec.
I would urge those federal members to come to Abitibi-Temiscamingue today and tell residents that federal participation and co-operation with their communities has been cut off. Mr. Speaker, they will get a warm welcome!

Mr. Speaker, in China it is almost June 4. Two years ago began one of the most horrific incidents of bloody, violent massacres by a government against its own people.
The scene was Beijing's Tiananmen Square, and overnight the Chinese government chose to end a peaceful youth protest by opening tank and machine gun fire upon the crowd of pro-democracy demonstrators.
What were the youth asking? Freedom from totalitarianism through political reform, more opportunity and personal dignity. In return, they were murdered. Some survivors of that horrible night have Subsequently been executed, incarcerated or, at the very minimum, stripped of basic human rights and dignity.
The repression continues. On the second anniversary of this massacre, I encourage the Secretary of State for External Affairs to take a look today at Canada's policy on China. Let us not follow the lead of the United States' by giving China most-favoured nation status.
June 3, 1991

The Canadian government has not followed through on its initial bold policy, and has changed little in Canada's relationship with the Government of China since the Tiananmen Square incident.
We must reaffirm our own commitment to democracy and freedom by standing with the Chinese people as they aspire to a way of life that Canadians take for granted.

Mr. Speaker, environmental degradation is killing children. According to the 1990 United Nations state of the environment report on children and the environment, every year 14 million children under the age of five die in the developing countries as a result of unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation, environmental pollution, common diseases and malnutrition. A further 3 million are seriously disabled.
In the industrialized countries, the main environmental source of death and disability among children is exposure to various forms of pollution and hazardous chemicals in the environment. Even the unborn are affected by chemicals in the air and toxic substances taken in through the mother's body.
As adults working together with the government and industry, we have both an opportunity and a responsibility to take advantage of current knowledge, technology and resources to improve the well-being of the world's children and the planet itself before it is too late.
Planet earth must be made a safe home for future generations.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council met with members of Parliament to discuss their concerns for the future of Canada and the right of ethnocultural minorities to be directly represented in the process of constitutional reform.
National unity requires an affirmation that all Canadians from diverse backgrounds are equal in a multicultural, multiracial Canada.
New Democrats support the CEC in its request for a representative constituent assembly and the addition of a strong Canada clause to our Constitution.
We also must actively counteract racism in Canada. Public education on the values of immigration and more positive media race relations are a first step. Employment equity must be mandatory. We need increased funding, especially in western Canada for English language programs. There must be amnesty for refugee claimants who have waited years in the backlog.
The many issues raised today prove once again how essential advocacy groups like CEC are to make our democracy work for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, students at Pleasant View Junior High School in Don Valley North, North York, are taking an impressive leadership role in ensuring that citizens today and tomorrow will have a healthy planet. This Thursday, June 6, they will be having a conference to spread their message to their elected representatives and children and parents in the Pleasant View family of schools.
Since 1989 they have a long list of projects they have accomplished, including recycling in various ways and composting of waste. The one thing I particularly like is an environmental assessment of every student's home, followed by a letter to Mom and Dad advocating a family meeting. This meeting resulted in a family action plan to improve relations with the planet.
They are also looking internationally. They have bought 25 acres of rain forest through the World Wildlife Fund and have purchased shares in the World Wildlife Fund's endowment program.
Congratulations on your leadership, Pleasant View students. Together we can have a green world.

Last week was National Access Awareness Week, a time when this government should have been sending out positive

June 3, 1991
messages of support to the disabled community. Actions, however, always speak louder than words.
The National People First project is a voice for developmentally handicapped people in this country. It is a self-help organization dedicated to the empowerment of developmentally handicapped persons to protect themselves against abuse and to assert their rights in the event that they have been abused.
National People First was funded by the Department of National Health and Welfare for six years, from 1984 to 1990. This funding has not been renewed for 1991 and the future of this movement looks bleak.
I call on the Minister of National Health and Welfare to live up to this government's commitment to support abuse prevention programs. I urge this government to allocate funds to this unique and invaluable organization so that the progress it has made will not be tragically lost.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the many British Columbians who live and work in the Fraser River watershed, I would like to commend the government for its $100 million commitment toward the cleanup of the Fraser. The Fraser is so much more than just a large river. It has become a barometer reflecting the state of British Columbia's environmental health.
This program, announced over the weekend, will be directed toward such high priorities as restored salmon populations, protection and restoration of fish and wildlife habitat, as well as monitoring and improvement of water quality.
The Fraser River is important to many British Columbians and they will recognize the significance of this initiative. But these same people are equally important to the health of the Fraser for it is their ideas and help that will ensure the effective and successful implementation of this plan to restore the Fraser River to its former greatness.
1991 CITATION FOR CITIZENSHIP AWARDS

Mr. Speaker, to be a citizen of Canada, whether by birth or by choice, involves the unwritten responsibility to contribute to the betterment of this country. Our society values freedom and participation and respects those who are willing to accept the responsibility of contributing.
Today, the 1991 Citation for Citizenship awards are being presented to 21 individuals and four organizations whose contributions to Canada merit national recognition. These people have given their time and energy to making Canada a better place in which to live. From health care to human rights, from education to multicul-turalism, every aspect of our society has been touched in some way by these dedicated Canadians.
I am sure that I can speak for all members in this House when I express our congratulations to the people and organizations honoured today. A citation for citizenship is a symbol of the gratitude that we feel toward these people and others like them all across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this was one of those "good news, bad news" weekends in north-western Ontario. First, the good news: Thanks to the efforts of the Ontario NDP government in securing a strictly commercial solution to the shut down of Atikokan Forest Products sawmill, we were able to announce the mill's reopening and, in fact, some workers started today and the rest of the 160 will be due next week.
Thanks, Ontario.
In Thunder Bay, the news was not as good. Abitibi Price arbitrarily closed its Thunder Bay paper mill for two years, putting 400 people out of work directly, with considerably more out of work indirectly. Both the Sapawe sawmill and the Thunder Bay paper mill suffer from the same federal government policies, softwood lumber tax, high Canadian dollar and high interest rates.
June 3, 1991

The federal Conservative government did not help Atikokan during its crisis. Will it help Thunder Bay? It better help.

Mr. Speaker, I remind all Canadians that the search for Raoul Wallenberg, one of Canada's two honorary citizens, goes on. This Swedish diplomat who disappeared in Hungary in 1945 saved as many as 20,000 Jews from Nazi death camps. Even though the Russians reported he died in 1947, Montreal lawyer Irwin Cotier of the International Commission searching for Wallenberg and members of the Wallenberg family itself still say there is no proof that he is dead.
Now highly supportive evidence says the Soviets offered to exchange Wallenberg for a Soviet spy jailed in Sweden in 1968, two decades after claiming he was dead. This only adds to reports of Wallenberg sightings in Soviet prisons in the 1980s and so we certainly hope that glasnost prevails as the search for clues in KGB files continues.
Luckily heroic efforts like Raoul Wallenberg's are remembered in the hearts of many for generations. I call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs to strongly urge Soviet co-operation in the search for Canada's honorary citizen whom we all admire.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are delighted to see the Prime Minister is back in the House. Canadians will now be able to rest easier, and let's hope he will stay in the country from now on.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. On Thursday of last week, the Minister of National Revenue said that the government has gone "too far", that Canadians are over-taxed and that the federal government should do something about it. On Friday, the Minister of Finance said Canadians are not over-
Oral Questions
taxed and so the government is not planning to do anything about it.
I ask the Prime Minister which minister is speaking for Canada on this issue, the Minister of National Revenue, who is right, or the Minister of Finance, who is wrong?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess I should start off by saying that nobody likes to pay taxes, but we must have taxes in this country to pay for the services that we all enjoy from being Canadians and living in this great country of ours.
If you compare Canada's taxes with those in the OECD, we are on average with them. Canada's tax burden today is about the same as it was in the early 1980s when the hon. Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Finance. The tax burden is vis-a-vis the same for the taxpayers of this country. Personal and corporate income taxes are higher in Canada than on the OECDwide basis. We will concede to that, but I can tell him that social security contributions by Canadians are less than half as burdensome in Canada than in other countries in the OECD.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance, the third Minister of Finance, or whatever he is, likes to compare Canada with other industrialized countries.
Today a study by Global Economics shows that taxes on individuals are higher in Canada than in any G-7 country. More than $1,500 in new taxex have been slapped on Canadian families since this government took office. The study concluded that today the system is more complicated than ever and less fair than ever.

Canada than in other countries in the OECD. Taxes have to be paid to pay the bills.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:

What is happening is that Mexico is opening up its borders and it is giving Canadian businesses new opportunities to get into Mexico to sell their goods and services there. That is what we are interested in, creating more jobs in Canada through sales to other countries, and Mexico is no exception.

Mr. Speaker, this government is as thick as a brick. What the Minister for International Trade said was very clearly that we should not try to compete with Mexico in areas where Mexico produces products. The issue very clearly is not whether our modem economy can compete with Mexico's Third World economy, as the minister said last week.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:

That is what it is all about.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.

A new study indicates today that in fact this government has continued that system of taxation, and there is no question that the tax system is a mess. The tax system is unfair. Mr. Speaker, what we have in front of us this afternoon is a bill which has some very serious dangers behind it, dangers which concern us as a party. It is clear to us that the question of transfer of airports to local authorities has not been thought through. It is clear that the tough questions about the national responsibility which has existed in the past for air transportation in this country and for facilities associated with air transportation have not been confronted by this government.
It seems to us that this is once more a question of an ideological commitment to doing away with as much community ownership as possible; control by society of elements which should be important parts of our communities' infrastructure.
Despite that sense of concern, that sense of real uncertainty about whether this government has thought this issue through, we are pleased to see a bill which does

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
try to lay out ways in which the workers involved in such transfers will be protected.
One of the things which is most devastating is to see privatizations take place and shutdowns occur and to see not the people who are responsible for those decisions taking the brunt of the difficulties of adjustment but the workers who have had no say in the decision themselves.
We have seen that with so many things which this government has done. We have seen it with free trade in which the great adjustment problems that the workers in this country have experienced in the context of free trade have not been dealt with by the government. Workers instead have been forced to carry those responsibilities themselves.
We have seen it with the shutdown of VIA Rail facilities in different parts of the country. We have seen it with respect to the CBC. Many parts of the country have experienced loss of CBC services, and workers have found themselves faced with the loss of jobs which they thought were jobs which were serving the community and which would continue to serve the community.
Yet the adjustment process has not been considered as a responsibility by government. Therefore, it is good to see a piece of legislation come before us which provides for some consideration with respect to employees' pensions and labour relations in connection with the transfer of some of the airports involved.
Nevertheless, even when we get to the question of how the workers affected in this case are themselves treated in this piece of legislation, there are some serious problems and some serious gaps which will lead us to vote for this referral back to committee. They will also lead us, assuming that vote is lost, to vote against third reading of this piece of legislation.
What is interesting is that there were some amendments that were suggested to this piece of legislation, some amendments which our labour critic, the member who sits beside me in the House here, put forward to the previous Minister of Transport, who is now the Solicitor General. One of those amendments suggested that in the event that employees are transferred to a designated airport authority prior to the negotiation of a new
collective agreement on behalf of their previous bargaining unit, the government will ensure that they receive any retroactive remuneration that they would otherwise have received for the period commencing on the date of expiry of their previous collective agreement until the date of their transfer to the designated local airport authority.
This in fact was quite a sensible amendment which was put forward.
The government indicated-and I have here the letter in which the previous Minister of Transport made this commitment on April 9, 1991-that there would be a change made which would effectively introduce that concept into this bill.
Now, the Solicitor General says that this was part of a deal. Let me suggest that if this was a sensible amendment which should have been part of the legislation and the government was prepared to put it into the legislation as part of a deal, surely it makes sense to put it into the legislation at this stage.
So that the minister's comments can be put quite carefully, this is a letter which was written to my colleague and I quote:
Dear Ms. Langan:
I am writing to you with respect to possible amendments to Bill C-85 -
Which is, of course, the new bill as it is now before us, Bill C-15.
-which you are considering proposing for Third Reading debate.
Departmental and Justice Canada officials have had an opportunity
to review the various draft amendments which you have made
available to us.
The minister then goes on to make his comments, and I hope that the minister would not suggest that I am misrepresenting the position which he took in this letter.
With respect to the second amendment which was put forward, our labour critic, on behalf of our party I might say, put forward the following suggestion that this should have an amendment with respect to clause 6 which would read as follows:
(4) Where an airport has been sold, leased or otherwise transferred to a designated airport authority, any designated employee for the airport shall retain the same rights and benefits as the designated employee enjoyed in the position held by the designated employee in the Public Service on the transfer date.
June 3, 1991

(5) The rights and benefits of a designated employee referred to in subsection (4) may not be altered or abrogated except pursuant to a new collective agreement that is binding on the designated employee, or, in the absence of any collective agreement binding on the designated employee pursuant to a decision made by the designated airport authority with respect thereto.
The minister continues to discuss this particular amendment and suggests that there may be some problems with the wording in subsection (5) and for that reason, it would not be acceptable to the government to accept that particular amendment.
There is a further amendment suggested by my colleague which, again, was not accepted.
The key point, however, is that the government was quite prepared, as given in this commitment from last April from the then Minister of Transport, to make some changes in this bill which would provide more protection for workers affected by this bill. One would have thought that in bringing this legislation back before us the government would have seen fit to see to it that these extra protections, which they were prepared to commit themselves to back last April, would be part of the new legislation.
Unfortunately that is not the case. This is yet a further reason, from our perspective as a party, to see this piece of legislation sent back to committee to consider some of the points put forward in the amendment which the Liberal Party has moved, and also to put at least one change into this piece of legislation which the previous Minister of Transport said he was prepared to do in order to provide a further safeguard for workers affected by this bill.
Without such changes, we have before us a piece of legislation which is faulty on a number of levels. It is faulty, first, because workers have not been consulted with respect to the changes which they would like to see in the legislation. The bill is in front of us. There has been no consultation with the the union of Transport Canada employees. What possible recipe for disastrous labour regulations could be chosen but to bring forward a piece of legislation meant to supposedly serve workers and not even to consult the union representing those
Government Orders
workers? What could possibly be achieved with that kind of approach?
What will be achieved will be a situation in which workers are affected by a bill and will feel aggrieved, almost regardless of what is in the legislation, because the bill has not been discussed with those workers.
Surely one thing we should have learned as members of Parliament trying to do something in this vast, difficult country is that no action is taken without consultation, without discussion.
I see the previous minister is here. I welcome him to participate in the debate, to stand up and explain why this particular piece of legislation was not discussed with the working people of the country. "Why were the working people affected by this bill not consulted", I ask the minister. If he says that the union of Transport Canada employees were in fact part of the process of negotiation and consultation that has taken place between Transport Canada and various local airport authorities, contrary to what I am told by our transport critic, I welcome the former minister to get up and make that point. I think it would be a valuable contribution. The procedural and substantive rights of workers with respect to their existing pensions are not clear under this bill.
That is not the first time we have seen this kind of reality emerge. We had to fight very hard to get pension rights established for workers when Canadian Arsenals, for instance, was privatized. We were successful in that case, but in this case the wording is not yet clear.
The bill needs to incorporate the desire of the workers to continue under the plans which they are presently part of as part of the Public Service. That is not just a sort of hypothetical question. The local airport authority in British Columbia is having difficulty finding an insurance company to take on the disability insurance plan which is currently provided to workers.
In short, we have a piece of legislation in front of us which, as usual with this government, betrays a lack of consultation, a lack of concern and a lack of responsibility to the working people of this country. For this reason, I hope very much that this House will accept the amendment which has been put before us to send this piece of legislation back to committee for certain types of review, and hopefully for other kinds of review as well.

If we do not do that, we will have broken faith with workers who have given many years to the airport authorities throughout this country.
