Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure today to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-15. My intervention today is veiy timely in that my riding is an area that is very rural in nature and has small airports. I know that a lot of members who have entered the debate so far continue to focus on the larger airports in the country and probably the ones that have more opportunity to make money.
My colleague, the member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, has made an amendment suggesting that we take a good look and make sure that the transfer of these particular facilities to airport commissions or to municipalities is not indeed privatization or selling of the facility.
That is a very important initiative. I think that if the intention of the government were to sell these facilities then truly there is an ulterior motive. There are some very grave difficulties with some of the airports in the areas that I am going to speak about.
One of the best ways I find to debate these issues is to pick a couple of examples and talk about those examples. That to me is an easier way of bringing the message across to our constituents and the people of Canada as to
Government Orders
what the difficulties are out there as they relate to Transport Canada, and specifically to airports in rural Canada.
Before I get to those specific examples, I want to talk about some of the issues that I think have to be addressed before we get into transferring these particular facilities to municipalities or airport commissions. First of all I must emphasize that this government and Transport Canada itself have to set up some guidelines. They cannot just hocus-pocus or holus-bolus take these airports, depending on their condition-and I will talk about that in more detail later-and decide to transfer them to particular communities without having at least minimum standards.
The guidelines for the transfer of airports have to be maintained across the board and they have to be decided upon based on population and based on size of airport. I know people will argue this point, but I am a firm believer that airports are used almost as political tools, as a slush fund to give this member of Parliament a brand new terminal this week because an election is coming up. That terminal, even if it is way oversized for that community, will be put there anyway to make that particular member look good in the eyes of his constituents.
We have that all across the country now. It has become very obvious, as I travel around the country, that the airport facilities of some communities are much better than those of other communities almost identical in size. That is why I think it is very important. If we are going to get into transferring all these facilities to the communities, first of all they should only be transferred if they meet certain guidelines. Those guidelines should be standard and meet the safety purposes that we as parliamentarians would like to see for the future of those airports.
Second, I think we should look very seriously at the guidelines and make sure that when we do transfer these airports, the employees who are being transferred with the facility are looked after in a way that is compatible with what we think is fair. Those individuals were Transport Canada employees all along for many years and all of a sudden became employees of a different type.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
We have to look at those very seriously. We also have to look at guidelines for capital improvements. It is very simple to transfer a facility, but not to discuss with Transport Canada the improvements of those facilities over a period of 5, 10, 15 and 20 years.
Without those kinds of guidelines, the community may be taking over a facility that is in good shape today but 10 years from now, when we want to improve our facility or to do some renovations, Transport Canada could easily say: "Well, we are sorry, we do not have the money any longer. You will have to go to the municipal taxpayer and get the dollars from them". That is a very sad and real issue that we will have to tackle before smaller communities would even consider taking on such an endeavour as running an airport.
We also need guidelines to make sure that we have increased funding for the maintenance agreements that we would be entering into.
One of the issues that hit home not too long ago in my riding was that Transport Canada put a freeze on the amount of dollars that it was going to allocate to the Dryden airport. The community said that it could not continue to run this facility with the amount of dollars being given to it. There has to be some sort of guideline or some sort of mechanism that would allow these communities, even though the airports are transferred, to be able to go to Transport Canada and the minister and suggest that because of some circumstances, there has to be an increase in funding in order to resolve those issues.
We are not all in the position, in these small airports in smaller towns and cities in Canada, to be able to make enough revenues from these particular facilities of not having to rely on the taxpayers of Canada, on Transport Canada, on the Ministry of Transportation in order to maintain these facilities in the way that we expect them to be maintained.
Those are a few guidelines that we have to set down if we are even going to consider transferring these facilities to smaller communities. If we are not going to put those kind of guidelines in place then this really is a scam. It is really saying to Canadians: "Listen, we do not want to be bothered any more with your airport facilities. We deregulated it for you. Told you that when we deregulated it the services would be better". That did not happen. "Well we deregulated this particular facility for you so that you would get lower fares". That did not happen. Now the government is saying: "Well, we cannot seem to run this facility very well as a government, we will give it to you at the local level and we are sure you can do a better job. But then again, do not come back to us at any time and suggest that we will protect you to a certain extent. You will just basically have to look after yourself."
That is not the kind of message I would hope that the government is sending to the small communities and the many, many small airports across this country.
Having said that, I want to give a few examples of some of the difficulties I see in transferring smaller rural airports. When I say smaller rural airports, I am talking about communities with 5,000 people, with 10,000 people and, in some cases, as in the one example I have in my hand, of a community of 22,000. Now this facility, when I describe what is wrong with it and the lack of guidelines and procedures that Transport Canada does not seem to have in place or, if it does, only in place where it feels that someone might be watching, it makes you kind of wonder just what the government has in mind.
Let me give an example of what is happening in a community of mine, Kenora, Ontario. Kenora has three communities in its area, Kenora, Keewatin and Jaffray-Melick. Those three communities have a population of roughly 22,000. You would think that there would be a pretty decent facility there with an area and a population of that size, not to mention that the population in the summertime blossoms to about 50,000 people. We are now talking about the tourism component of an area like Kenora-Rainy River, which is probably one of the most beautiful parts of Ontario and, indeed, probably one of the most beautiful parts of Canada.
This airport that I am talking about has a maintenance agreement with hours of operation of 42.5 hours per week. Everyone says: "Well, that is not too bad when you consider that roughly most airports run on a hundred hours a week" and people will ask: "Well, what seems to be the problem?"
Let me give an example. There are four other airports on my list and I will just list them: Dryden, Sioux Lookout, Red Lake and Fort Frances. Those are four
June 3, 1991

other communities of my riding. All have smaller populations than the one I am talking about.
Sioux Lookout receives funding for 15 hours a day, seven days a week which works out to 105 hours per week. That is over double the amount of hours and maintenance dollars given to the community of Sioux Lookout compared to the community of Kenora.
Red Lake is funded for 12 hours a day from Monday to Friday which is 60 hours per week.
Fort Frances has a maintenance operating agreement for 14 hours a day, seven days a week, which is 98 hours per week.
Atikokan, which is another one I did not mention, has 84 hours per week.
Those four or five communities all have double and some almost triple amounts of hours per week in funding for maintenance agreements which are signed with different governments, not all federal, some provincial. They have different agreements with senior levels of government to operate their facilities.
I have difficulty understanding where Transport Canada is coming from when looking at the facilities, the population and the potential of these different communities and their maintenance agreements.
I am very pleased that a community like Dryden gets 105 hours per week of operation dollars in its maintenance agreement.
That kind of facility is necessary in a community like Dryden. However, then there is a community like Kenora which has double the population, almost triple the population of a community like Dryden but has half the maintenance agreement that this community has.
You say to yourself: "Well, what does that mean, operating cost?" Let me put it in dollars and cents. That is a good way to explain to our residents and constituents what it means. It is right here. I will just quickly grab it for you. It explains in detail the operating costs.
Kenora in 1988-89 had an operating cost, money that it was given by the federal government, of $204,000 and made revenues of roughly $131,000 for a cost recovery of 64.5 per cent.
Government Orders
Dryden had an operating cost of $897,000 from money that was given by the federal government with revenues of $308,000 for a recovery of 34.4 per cent.
Fort Frances had operating costs of $273,500 and revenues of $81,000 for a cost recovery of 29.8 per cent.
I guess you are sitting there thinking: "Well, what are you getting at?" Let me tell you what I am getting at. The fact remains is that, if you are familiar with the region, the community of Kenora and the airport is a very essential component of that community's long term goals and hopes and aspirations for the future. Now, Transport Canada in its wisdom treats that particular airport much differently than it treats the one down the road a hundred miles. We cannot understand for the life of us why that is.
There cannot be any reason other than there are political decisions being made as to whether to fund a particular airport or to not fund a particular airport. It cannot be used as an argument that this airport is any less important than the other, considering that the population is double the size of the other communities that I mentioned.
I want to switch to the other example because I know I will end up running out of time as I usually do. I want to talk a little bit about another airport, the Sioux Lookout airport.
In March 1990, the town of Sioux Lookout submitted an application under the Local/Local Commercial Airports Financial Assistance Program to the minister. This Local/Local Commercial Airports Financial Assistance Program is run directly through the Minister of Transport, which means that when you apply for this program, in order to get assistance to improve your airport, you have to convince the minister and not Transport Canada of the importance of this particular project and whether he should fund it.
The town of Sioux Lookout went to the minister for this application. It was the previous minister. I will explain why this community went for these improvements and I will give some statistics just to show what has happened, but before I do that, let me give the groundwork.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
This is a community of about 5,000 people. Why would a community of 5,000 need a large airport? This particular community is the jump-off point to go up north, to northern Ontario and to all the isolated aboriginal communities of practically half of Ontario. People fly out of this particular airport and go to that region which has, roughly speaking, about 10,000 aboriginal people. They have no alternative but to go by air for medical purposes and to get to the outside world, unless you consider a canoe or a dog sled to be a good alternative. That is the only possible way to get to Thunder Bay or Winnipeg, to fly out of there over to Sioux Lookout and from there transfer and on to points west or east.
Let me show the traffic trends. This particular community has increased seven fold in traffic in the last 10 years. It is the busiest airport in north-western Ontario, next to Thunder Bay. Thunder Bay has a population of over 100,000 people and this particular community of
5.000	has a large amount of traffic coming out of it.
In 1977, 8,100 passengers used the airport. In 1988, the number almost reached 50,000 passengers. It is estimated that by the year 2001, more than 60,000 passengers will use the airport. When the airport was built in the early 1970s, it was built for 8,000 passengers, it is now almost at 50,000 passengers and is expected to see over
60.000	passengers by the year 2001.
What did the minister say? He said: "We do not have the funding right now. You are not high on the priority list, therefore maybe you can apply next year and you will have to live with the airport you have". We are not talking about service to one community. We are talking about people from 30 communities who come from the far north to this airport and we cannot even get it on the priority list so that somewhere down the line we can tell all those communities in north-western Ontario that they will have a decent airport facility.
In that airport there is not even a confectionery, there is not even a place to grab a sandwich. There is a bubble gum machine, a place where you can buy cigarettes- heaven forbid-and a place where you can buy chocolate bars and chips and that is all. There are almost 50,000 people using that facility already. There is a population explosion going on in the north and I am sure they will continue to use it.
The only alternative is for the Minister of Transport to build us a road up north.
Those are two examples that I think bring to light the issue of how important it is to understand where the Ministry of Transport is going, before we start transferring these airports to municipalities and to the individual communities. Is it suggesting that it does not want to get involved in the future of these particular communities and their airports? Is it suggesting that it cannot afford it at the federal level? Is it saying: "You look after it municipally or provincially, or to hell with you?" I get the impression that is the kind of scenario we are looking at.
I think we are quite prepared as communities to take over these airports.
If we are given the proper guidelines, if you are quite honest and frank with us and tell us just what you are proposing to do as far as a long term capital for the improvements of these facilities, and if you are prepared to give us the kind of guidelines to help with the employee transfers and make sure that they get the same kind of benefits they got before, then I think we as a party will be prepared to take a good look at it.
First of all I think we have to clear up the most important part of this whole bill, and I was so very impressed that the member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon brought it up: We must make sure that this is not a privatization but a transfer of facilities, if the communities can come to some sort of understanding of just what the transfer means to them and if it is an improvement to them.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying a few words about this legislation. The reason why I do so is because Canadians must be wondering what is
June 3, 1991

going on. Are we talking about taking all of our airports in Canada and passing them over to organizations?
I picked up a brochure which says "airport transfer." It shows a picture of an aeroplane leaving an airport, and in the middle of it is the Maple Leaf; "Airport transfer, Transport Canada". I read these words in this brochure and I want to put this on the record: "The broad objectives of the policy are (1) to allow national airport systems to operate in a more cost-efficient manner."
If that were not enough, further down it says: "Key elements of the policy specify that federal funding requirements will not increase."
Finally: "Each LAA (local airport authority) will be an independent, incorporated business entity and will finance its operating and capital needs without recourse to the federal government."
In other words, we have a bill being passed in this House right now that will pass Canada's airports over to local authorities which are supposed to find the money to operate them and the capital expenditures to build new runways without recourse to the federal government to pay the bills. It is an interesting proposition.
I looked at the bill a moment ago and it is rather a strange one. I have the secret copy here, that is, the copy that came out before the other copies, I suppose. It should be called "secret" because what is in the bill is really a secret. I cannot figure out what is in the bill. I have looked at it and I cannot figure out what is in it. It says here that it is an act to provide for certain matters respecting official languages. Official languages; I looked in the bill and in the section under "official languages" it says that parts 4, 8, 9 and 10 of the Official Languages Act apply. The really relevant parts in the Official Languages Act are parts 5 and 6. We assume from this legislation then that parts 5 and 6 do not apply. If the other parts are singled out as applying, then the other parts of the Official Languages Act do not apply to the transfer of airports.
If it is the law of the land that the Official Languages Act applies to all the airports in Canada then the bill has to be rewritten. Montreal is changing hands and is no longer being operated by the federal government. Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary are changing and are no
Government Orders
longer federal government airports. I believe the others are Edmonton and Calgary. Then there is a whole bunch of airports like Moncton and several others that are also going to be transferred from federal hands. The federal government will no longer be operating them.
This is certainly confusing here where it says an act respecting official languages and then it says employees' pensions. I looked up the clause affecting employees' pensions and it said in that regard: "The Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the President of the Treasury Board", and the Governor in Council is what the layman would call the cabinet, "make regulations (a) respecting the manner in which" the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act will apply.
In other words, there is nothing at all in the bill that deals with employees' pensions. There is not a thing. It says that the government will make regulations after the bill is passed in relation to employees' pensions.
One might ask how an employee of an airport, who is no longer a public servant because it is now passed over to a public authority to operate it, can come under the Public Service Superannuation Act anyway. He is no longer a public servant. How can that individual come under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act when he is no longer a public servant?
The truth of the matter is that you need not be a public servant to come under the Public Service Superannuation Act. Petro-Canada employees are under that act. The post office is under that act. The Occupational Health and Safety Branch of the federal government is under that act. They are not really public servants and they need not be either.
I suppose it is rather confusing to the layman, but the Canadian Union of Public Employees and the Public Service Alliance of Canada can also represent them even though they are not public servants. It sounds strange, does it not, to have the Public Service Alliance of Canada represent somebody who is not a public servant? But that is the way it goes. It represents people in Crown corporations, for example. The Canadian Union of Public Employees represents employees who are not public employees.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
Nowhere in the act does it talk about and spell out the employees' pensions. That is two gone now: an act to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, but there is nothing in there to cover official languages, and then it says employees' pensions but there is nothing in there to cover employee pensions. There is a section that says the government may make regulations respecting employees' pensions.
The last part mentions labour relations in connection with the transfer of certain airports. I looked up the section under labour relations and it says that the whole matter will be passed over to the Canada Labour Relations Board. I can recall when the post office was passed over to the Canada Labour Relations Board. There were two years of status quo and then the Canada Labour Relations Board was supposed to determine the bargaining agents and the unions representing the employees. They have been at it now for nine years, and they still have not decided the question of bargaining units and bargaining agents.
I do not know why the government presented the bill to the House. What it means by official languages is confusing. It does not talk about employees' pensions and labour relations is left to the Canadian Labour Relations Board, so what is the purpose of the legislation?
To find the purpose of the legislation, of course, we can look at the brochure called "Airport Transfer". I asked for and received, a few moments ago, the outline of what is called the supplementary principles of airport transfer.
In other words, you have all of these airports in Canada now being passed over to local authorities. You have all of these employees in Canada who have families, who have been working for the federal government for years, wondering: "What is going to become of me and my job?", and then you have the travelling public who is landing at those airports. They are wondering: "Should I be landing at this airport? What kind of an airport is this? Does it have federal standards? If the plane catches fire, who is going to put out the fire? Whose standards are they? Are they good standards?" You have two of those concerns.
I had sent to me the actual list of supplementary principles which have now been sent to all of these airports. I want to put a couple of them on the record.
First of all, the federal government says that inspection agencies like customs and excise, immigration, health and welfare and agriculture will be provided free of charge to the Crown by the local airport authority. Then it says: "The local airport authority will provide at no cost to Transport Canada space requirements for such services as air navigation free of charge to the federal government."
It says that as far as the employees are concerned: "In any case, all terminated Transport Canada Public Service employees, whether or not they transfer to the LAA," that is the local airport authority, "have a right to have their name placed on the priority list for one year. More particularly, employees who were laid off by the LAA," local airport authority, "up to the end of the first year after the date of transfer would benefit from placement on the priority list."
In other words, Mr. Speaker, you could have an employee or employees terminated with no rights to any other job in the federal government, would lose his or her seniority rights, would lose all of their benefits, would have no more standing than a member of Parliament as an airport employee.
Then the ultimate of all of the regulations. I want to highlight this condition: "The LAA as operators," that is, the local airport authority, "will ensure the provision of crash, fire and rescue services at the airport." That is quite a statement. The local airport authority as operators will ensure the provision of crash, fire and rescue services. The LAA will development emergency and contingency plans, conduct exercises among the various jurisdictions and operating entities, for example, police, ambulance, hospitals and airlines.
The whole operation of the airport, including the fire department is being passed over to the local airport authority. Then it says the local airport authority will be responsible for dealing with air pollution, solid waste management and other airport related environmental issues. That is quite a change for Canadian airports. All airports in all of those communities across Canada will be passed from the federal government to a local authority and that local authority will ensure the safety of the travelling public. The only thing the federal government will do, according to these guidelines, is guard against terrorism and provide air traffic control services.
June 3, 1991

That is quite a change for Canada's airports, isn't it? That is quite a change. How do you provide, as a local airport authority, all of the policing that is required at international airports, for example? How do you provide for all of the environmental checks and balances that are required at every airport in this country?
The bottom line is that the federal government, in presenting the bill to this Chamber, and saying that it is a bill respecting employees' pensions and labour relations, and yet not having it in the bill what it is going to do, the federal government in passing over to local authorities responsibilities that should be nation wide and responsibilities by the Government of Canada.
Finally, the federal government is saying to every single airport employee in this country that the day is going to come for some of them immediately, when you will no longer be an employee of the federal government, when you will no longer have seniority rights, or sick leave, or vacation benefits. "We are going to transfer all of that", as the brochure says, "to operate in a more cost efficient manner", and then to say that "the LAA will be an independent incorporated business entity and will finance its operations and capital needs without recourse to the federal treasury". The bottom line is that the federal government is trying to get out of the business of transportation in this country.
The only thing that I can see moving this policy is the efforts of the Government of Canada to try to save money in every single area of responsibility that it presently has, and to pass all of that responsibility over on to someone else's shoulders. In the case of an environmental issue at one of our airports, say, with noise pollution, the federal government will very shortly say: "Too bad, but that is the responsibility of a group of businessmen in that community because they actually own the airport". If they do not own the airport, then why is it that they are responsible for environmental matters and noise pollution?
The government will be able to say to the Auditor General: "We are getting rid of thousands of employees next year. We have reduced the Public Service by thousands of people, because we erased all of those thousands of people working at airports in Canada". The
Government Orders
travelling public, when they learn and when they hear on the news media about the firefighters at the airport saying: "We want to still stay in a federal system. We want to have our federal standards maintained". Someone will say: "Yes, they are still federal standards, it is just you are not a federal employee any more. You are operated by some incorporated body in the community of such and such".
The federal government should rethink this. I do not think they should bring a bill which does not guarantee a man his job after this is passed. I do not think we should allow them to pass a bill that does not guarantee a man or woman their pension after working at an airport in this country for the past 20 or 25 years. I do not think that we should allow the Government of Canada to cop out on its responsibility to provide security and environmental protection for the people of Canada at Canadian airports.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few brief words about Bill C-15, legislation introduced this past session. Before I start my comments, I would like to compliment the critic from our party, the member from Thunder Bay who, has led a lot of the debate on this particular legislation and to thank yourself, Mr. Speaker, for this opportunity to say a few words.
Bill C-15 is one of these interesting administrative pieces of legislation, I suppose. You look at the title and read through it and wonder exactly what is the purpose of the bill. You usually have to have a stack of other bills and information at hand to try and figure out what is happening. I guess as a short description of the legislation, the purpose of the bill is to protect essentially the collective bargaining rights, language rights and pension rights of federal public sector workers currently employed by Transport Canada during the transfer to airports from Transport Canada to local airport authorities, the LAAs that we have heard about.
You will be familiar with some of the attempts by this government to basically, privatize if you like, or localize the airport authority. The running and managing of a particular airport, is transferred to a local organization. I understand from some of the notes, in fact, it is being attempted for the first time in Edmonton.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
In any case, this legislation attempts to ensure that when that is the case, that employees who will then start becoming employees of that local authority will be protected by some of the benefits they have now in their collective agreement under federal legislation.
While the general thrust of the bill is good, it suffers from a lack of clarity and in light of current worker-management relations, it does not provide the protection it purports to provide.
I would like to go through a couple of the points that have been raised by the union that represents the employees, the Union of Transport Canada Employees. They have cited a number of very important aspects of the bill that I think will obviously have to be addressed.
The first one is that workers or their representatives have not really been a part of the process of negotiation and consultation that has gone on between Transport Canada and various local airport authorities.
That has become an unfortunate aspect of legislation under this government. I think it is important that the government attempt to establish good employer-employee relationships, that the employees are taken into consideration and are given every opportunity to see in advance what is being planned in any particular legislation and especially a case that affects their future, their occupation, their livelihood and for many people, their pensions.
The procedural and substantive rights of workers with regard to their existing pensions under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act are actually not clear under the bill. It is being left up to Treasury Board to make regulations. There has been no consultation on the development of these regulations.
I would hope that every effort is made, when new regulations are developed that the employees have ample opportunity to comment on that.
It is increasingly a part of legislation in our country that a bill gives a general mandate and instructions to government. However, in reality the real nitty-gritty of a law comes in the development of regulations which are developed by the department and eventually approved by the Governor in Council and by cabinet. I think it
takes a generous government to give the people an opportunity for input. It also requires a vigilant public, employees group or union to see that when those proposed regulations come forward they are looked at, circulated and considered.
The bill needs to incorporate the desires of workers to continue under these plans. I mentioned earlier the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act.
We understand that the local authority in British Columbia is having some difficulty in trying to find an insurance company to take on the disability component and the plan that is currently provided workers. They have been told that it would be too expensive to continue this type of coverage.
Point number three. The continuation of the bargaining agent is also a matter of great concern. The bill provides for the continuation of the terms and conditions of an existing collective agreement at the time of transfer. However, past experience with other privatizations demonstrates that the determination of the appropriate bargaining agent is a very long and disruptive process.
The bill should incorporate provisions so that the existing bargaining agent remains in place for the period of one full collective agreement after the transfer, in order to ensure the protection of worker's rights and the orderly determination of a bargaining agent.
That sounds like a pretty logical way to approach this particular idea. It gives the workers and the employer a chance to know that there is a grace period prior to, likely, some initiatives from an employer. We would probably expect that. They might not be good initiatives, but under law employers certainly would be allowed to do that. Of course, the employees who have a new employer, obviously as time advances would be looking to approach that employer for new provisions in any collective agreement they have.
The bill fails to make clear that all services to the travelling public will continue to be provided in both official languages. One of the proposals is to ensure that any third parties who are under contract to the airport authority are required to provide their services under the linguistic terms currently set out the Official Languages Act and any regulations made under that act.
June 3, 1991

That is a matter of a great deal of concern for some of the members of the House who have pursued this particular issue a great deal. Obviously, when we travel a lot as most members do, we realize that it is important that standards developed from airport to airport should be the same. It makes for ease of travel and ensures that people travelling from one airport to another understand safety requirements and public notices, and the employees who provide that service can assist them the best they can.
Just as an aside, what bugs me is that there are different TV monitors in each airport. Trying to read the monitors in some of the airports, trying to figure out which airline and which aeroplane is landing at what time, is difficult. I know that is a fairly minor point, given the importance of this legislation. I suppose I will suffer along. However, it is obviously a small example of the kind of general services we would like to see from airport to airport.
The general theme of Bill C-15 is that this may not be the privatization of airports, but it is certainly privatization of the workplace. The government has a responsibility to ensure the rights of its workers are protected before and after the transfer.
In the United States, after its rush with deregulation, and now in Canada, we were told just a short time ago that with deregulation we would have all these new airlines and new services. Well, we are right down to two airlines now. Some are suggesting that we may end up with only one airline in the future. The point I am making is that there is no guarantee that once the local authority takes over and runs one of these facilities that it is actually going to do a good job of it.
We certainly hope it does, but as the public trustee of Canada's airports, obviously the federal government must have in the back of its mind at least a back-up plan to reassume control of a particular airport if it does not work. Then we would be looking at taking care of employees' various benefits and rights as well as if the government was to resume control.
The bill gives only more uncertainty. If the purpose is to stabilize worker-management relations, then the workers must be consulted and their concerns heeded. We have to underline that point. Too often when a
Government Orders
number of these projects go ahead, we end up with bad labour relations. That is not going to be any help at all to our airports.
We are supporting the bill. We have some concerns, obviously, about what the government is planning to do. There are some very clear concerns that we have laid out and there have been comments made in the House by other members concerning employee relations. We feel that is important. We certainly hope the government will consider those in the future in the management of these airports. We respectfully ask these new authorities, when they are the employer, to treat their employees well.

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to take part in the debate on Bill C-15, an Act to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, employees pensions and labour relations in connection with the transfer of certain airports.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 contains an issue which is of particular interest to me. I will focus my remarks on clause 4 of the bill, which deals with official languages.
Clause 4(1) states that:
Where the Minister has sold, leased or otherwise transferred an airport to a designated airport authority, on and after and transfer date Parts IV, VIII, IX and X of the Official Languages Act apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, to the authority in relation to the airport as if
(a)	the authority were a federal institution; and
(b)	the airport were an office or facility of that institution, other than its head or central office.

Mr. Speaker, subsection 4(2) also recalls that nothing in subsection 23(2) of the Official Languages Act shall, in relation to an airport transferred to a designated airport authority by the Minister, be construed or applied so as to impose a duty on any institution other than that authority.

Clause 4 is sufficiently ambiguous to bring into question whether official languages regulations will be fulfilled at any airport which has been transferred to a non-governmental authority.

June 3, 1991
Government Orders
In subclause (1) only parts 4, 8, 9 and 10 of the Official Languages Act will apply.
In subclause (2) one is left wondering if certain parts of the Official Languages Act will only apply to the airport authority itself and not to other aspects or other individuals involved with the operation of that airport after the transfer has occurred.
The Liberal Party opposes the privatization of Canadian airports. However, we do support initiatives to transfer the administration and management of airports to local authorities under certain conditions.
One of these conditions is that the Official Languages Act apply in full to the local authority and its employees, and as well to services provided at the airport which has been transferred.
Bill C-15 leaves too much doubt as to the full application of the Official Languages Act upon the local airport authority, the employees of that authority and to the various services that will be provided to the public at the airport. Section 10 of the Air Canada Public Participation Act clearly sets out that the entire Official Languages Act would continue to apply to Air Canada, its employees and the services it renders after its privatization.
Bill C-15 does not extend the same stipulation concerning the full involvement of the Official Languages Act as does the Air Canada Public Participation Act of 1988. As a result, one questions why this is the case.
The Official Languages Act has 12 parts, yet Bill C-15 only includes parts 4, 8, 9 and 10. Part 4 deals with communications with, and services to, the public. Part 8 involves responsibilities and duties of Treasury Board in relation to the Official Languages Act of Canada. Part 9 concerns the commission of official languages and part 10 provides for court remedy. It is understandable why all these parts are worthy of inclusion in Bill C-15.
Obviously, one can understand why certain parts of the Official Languages Act are not included in Bill C-15. Some, such as parts 1, 2, 3, 11 and 12 are non-applicable as they deal with such matters as the proceedings of Parliament and the administration of justice. However, it is not clear as to why parts 5, 6 and 7 have been excluded from this piece of legislation.
Each one of these three parts are important components in our official languages legislation. Part 5 deals with the language of work, part 6 concerns the participation of English and French speaking Canadians and part 7 concerns the advancement of English and French. Certainly these are important issues.
In addition, parts 5 and 6 are designed to protect workers of both linguistic groups. Part 5, as I have said, has the mandate to protect the language of work, while part 6 protects equal opportunity to gain employment.
It is very difficult to determine the reasons behind their exclusion from Bill C-15. Why, indeed, were they left out of this legislation, but included in the Air Canada bill? Why should workers at Air Canada be protected and not workers at Canada's airports? Both institutions offer somewhat similar services to the public across the country.
Furthermore, the removal of part 7 is of equal concern. The exclusion of this part removes the right of the Department of Secretary of State to encourage and co-operate with both the provinces and the public to accomplish the objectives given to it by the Official Languages Act. This mandate is to enhance the vitality of English and French linguistic minorities throughout Canada and foster the full recognition and use of both official languages in Canada. I cannot think of any worthy reason as to why the minister would omit such an important part of the Official Languages Act from Bill C-15.
I would like for the minister to inform this House why his government does not want parts 5, 6 and 7 of the Official Languages Act to apply to local airport authorities and their employees. Has the government taken a change in course concerning official bilingualism in this country? Are they prepared to safeguard and protect the federal principle of bilingualism in all of its relevant legislation or in just some?
These are very important questions and Canadians want the answers.
We have a case here in Bill C-15 where vital parts of Canada's Official Languages Act are being excluded from legislation which should contain them.
The fact that these three parts of the Official Languages Act are, indeed, excluded from Bill C-15 is even further cause for concern given the current constitutional climate in Canada. How can this government talk of
June 3, 1991

fairness, equality and national identity one day and then turn around and introduce this legislation the next? The government cannot afford jeopardizing national reconciliation and preserving Canada's linguistic duality by watering down the objectives of the Official Languages Act.
The government cannot pick and choose which parts of the Official Languages Act it will include and what parts it will leave out of legislation, such as the one before this House today. The parts in question are not inconsequential, they are very important.
While there were obvious reasons for omitting certain parts of the Official Languages Act, as I have discussed earlier, there are no valid reasons I can think of to justify the removal of parts 5, 6 and 7 from Bill C-15.
I would like to conclude by quoting from the remarks made by the Commissioner of Official Languages when he appeared before the committee of the House of Commons responsible for examining Bill C-85, the designation given to Bill C-15 in the last session. At that meeting on March 7, 1991, the Commissioner said:
That section 4 of Bill C-85 be amended to ensure that, as in the case of the decisions taken in the privatization of Air Canada, all the provisions of the Official Languages Act continue to apply to the designated airport authorities. Any weakening of this policy would seem to us to be an unacceptable and unjustified step backward.
I believe the Commissioner speaks for all Canadians on this issue and I fully concur with his recommendation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to speak on Bill C-15, which is the Airport Transfer Act. I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this particular bill. It has been one of considerable concern to me since I was elected.
I have been in constant pursuit of the three various ministers who have been appointed since the election in 1988, to discuss not only the transfer of airports but also
a number of components that deal in particular with transportation in the north.
We have a government in the Northwest Territories that has quite handily carved out a fairly comprehensive transportation strategy that includes and probably compliments the whole issue of airport transfer. In fact they have gone one step further to deal not only with the transfer of airports but also with communications and the whole issue of safety.
In the north the majority of the population is highly dependent on air travel. Considering that particular concern, my constituents in the Northwest Territories have specific concerns that they want to share with the authorities that be. They want those concerns to be made known to the minister who has the authority and the department officials who have the responsibility.
In particular, there has been much concern with the transfer of airports that not only is there a priority list of communities that would have their airports upgraded before the transfer was made, but also that there are communities which need complete refurbishing or rebuilding of their airports.
An example-it is not only one-would be Fort Franklin which has its own airport located right at the end of the schoolyard. When you fly into the community of Fort Franklin, the minister should know that you fly over a schoolyard and a school. This is quite a dangerous situation if we talk about safety.
There has been much of a push over the last four or five years by this community to have a complete relocation.
This is not the only community. There are other communities that asked for a complete rebuilding mostly because of safety.
The other thing that the northerners, my constituents, would like the authorities to know is that we have currently the proposal to build a new terminal in the very busy community of Norman Wells.
A cost analysis team went in, but the cost analysis has not been returned to the community. In the greater scheme of things across Canada, on an economy of scale, the northerners feel they are not at the top of the list of priorities.

They feel they would not want to miss the opportunity for this proposal to go forward. That is one particular concern which they want to be made known.
When I am speaking about the transfer of airports, I also want to speak about the conditions of some of these airports. These responsibilities have been transferred but to the over all infrastructure, upkeep and refurbishing of this infrastructure, the costs are prohibitive.
It is very expensive in the north and the amount of use that these particular airports get is very high because many of these communities rely solely on air travel. They do not have highways or railways attaching them to the outer communities.
These are expressed concerns. With the main carriers that land in some of our main terminals throughout the Mackenzie Valley, specifically in my area, we find that on the whole issue of official bilingualism we have taken it one step further.
Canadian Airlines should be applauded for the steps it has taken by way of tapes and technology to serve the people in that area in various languages. It serves the people in Inuktitut, Chippewan and in all the Dene languages.
It has been quite innovative and quite ingenious in the way it has done that. I would like to take the opportunity to applaud this type of activity which has been undertaken by a particular carrier.
I have one other concern. If you are a northerner you may have had the opportunity for the government to have transferred the authority to the Northwest Territories for airports. We have little power when it comes to the kind of services we receive at those particular airports from the main carriers.
For instance, if you live in the Northwest Territories you will notice that when the schedules have changed through the two main airlines service is reduced. It is impossible for the working public in the north to get out of Yellowknife, the capital of the north, on a Sunday.
On a Sunday, a working individual travelling to the east must leave the Northwest Territories at 9 a.m. and arrive perhaps at a destination of Ottawa at 9 p.m. or 10 p.m. That is a complete day of travel.
Government Orders
If that is not your preferred choice, you could leave Yellowknife at 7.30 in the evening, wait in Edmonton until a quarter to or twenty to one the next morning, take the all night flight and travel from Edmonton to Ottawa to arrive 8.05 bleary eyed and ill prepared for a full day of work.
It has been extremely difficult for the working and travelling public to appreciate the kind of situations that have arisen every time the schedule is changed. We appreciate the service. We know it is far better than we had 10 or 20 years ago, but still we believe that every time the schedule is changed, service is reduced.
We want to say that we are appreciative that our government in the Northwest Territories has essentially taken on the responsibility. We have a lot of reservations about the prohibitive costs it entails when a program is transferred and the authority is taken over. It is one thing to have the authority, but it is quite another thing to have adequate resources, not only to upkeep, maintain and to refurbish, but to completely relocate for the purposes of safety.
Since we have a new minister, many of my constituents have urged me to welcome this minister to come to our communities and to have a look and see the conditions that exist there. We would like to extend an invitation to the minister and to the senior officials to come and meet with our chiefs and our people who have concerns, and to meet with the Government of the Northwest Territories, if it so desires.
I just want to take the opportunity with regard to National Access Awareness Week last week to raise an issue of particular concern. I was honorary chair for the disabled in my area and I believe that as much as possible, although we live in the remotest parts of Canada, we have to make accommodations for the disabled, we have to ensure that there is mobility where it is possible and if there are additional costs, that those have to be incurred. Those people have to be put on an equal level with everyone else in terms of mobility and accessibility.

-this act will not have the kind of impact on municipal or regional airport authorities that one would like to see in this country, in relation to a service that we feel is an essential one for Canadian travellers. Clause 4 of Bill C-15 now before the House provides that only four of the twelve parts of the Official Languages Act will apply.
Mr. Speaker, I can understand why Parts I, II, III, XI and XII of the Official Languages Act do not apply but I find it hard to understand why Parts V, VI and VII do not, and I intend to explain to the House the impact of this oversight or this government decision not to include Parts V, VI and VII.
Mr. Speaker, Parts V and VI of the Official Languages Act are designed to protect employees belonging to the two language groups, in other words, to respect their legal right to work in the official language of their choice, which may be English in Montreal, where the majority official language might be French, and French in Winnipeg, for instance, when the majority official language is English.
Mr. Speaker, the idea is to allow any Canadian to work for an institution as important as a company dedicated to public transportation, and to obtain from that agency and its managers the right to work in the official language of their choice. Yet, there is no such guaranty in the legislation before us.
Part V protects the language in the workplace, whereas Part VI ensures equal employment opportunities. We have discussed this on second reading and in committee. Mr. Speaker, we have tried to convince the government of the importance of that issue, but our requests have fallen in deaf ears. That is why we are back, in third reading, after a rather short debate-let's face it-because the government has used a rather unusual procedure. The government has reinstated, so to speak, the bill in this third session of Parliament when, normally,
this legislation, which was not passed during the second session of the House, should have died on the Order Paper after the House prorogued, and should therefore have followed the normal legislative process afterwards.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that Parts V and VI are important to us because, in our opinion, they deal with the most fundamental issues, that is the rights of individual, the rights of Canadians to equal employment opportunities but also the right to work in federal institutions in the language of their choice. We objected to several aspects of this bill. There is of course the issue of official languages, the Official Languages Act, and I have another objection, reflected in the motion we tabled which was voted down. In this motion we asked the government, quite appropriately, to remove that part of the bill concerning the sale of airports. I know this is all over and done with, but I was really very disappointed to see that the government was so emphatic about keeping the word "sell" in the bill.
Why? Because when I sat on the committee, the government said: We have no intention of selling. So why put this word in the bill? Are we being overcautious? I don't think so. Are we being overly suspicious of a government that told us the GST would be a visible tax and a revenue neutral? Are we too suspicious of this government when it says that we must stop selling arms outside the country while proposing a bill aimed at doing just that?
Are we too suspicious of this government, Mr. Speaker, when it says that we must sell Canada abroad, in the other countries, in order to present it in a flattering light, while the Prime Minister is a little too critical of Ontario following its last budget?
Are we too suspicious of this government when it speaks about reconciliation between provinces while trying to create a new department? I think it is about the fortieth department in charge of regional development in Quebec, created I might add without consulting the province.
So, I wonder, are we too suspicious of the government when it uses the expression "has sold-an airport", even though we are told today that it is not considering selling any airport?
June 3, 1991

I don't know whether or not we are too suspicious, but the government is neglecting a good opportunity to say: "Yes, you are right, we do not need to use the word "sold" in the bill, this is an oversight on our part." Well,
I don't think it is an oversight, Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is all planned. We are not yet privatizing airports. For the time being it is only privatization of the workplace, of all services inside airports. However, with the word "sold" in the bill, privatization through sale of airports to private companies is only a question of time.
This is why I object to this bill and why I support the hon. member's motion. I think he is right to oppose the inclusion of the word "sold" in this bill.
I would like to talk about another objection I raised in the committee this bill was referred to and it concerns the official languages.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is a slap in the face of all Canadians with regards to official languages. I have always maintained-and I know some hon. members opposite have come to the realization-that, wherever you are in Canada, whether you are francophone or anglophone, services have to be provided in both languages. This is, essentially, what I think tourists and Canadians alike see as typical of Canada. We have two languages. Why? Because there are two groups of taxpayers: the English-speaking taxpayers and the French-speaking taxpayers.
So, on the subject of official languages, we should have the right to be served in the language of our choice anywhere in Canada, without exception. As a Quebecer, I can tell you that I am proud because, in Quebec, we have always respected the other language. Yes, there were clashes here and there, but on the whole we show due consideration for the language of the minority, the English language. But when it comes to federal institutions, I find it very important to preserve the intent of the Official Languages Act and to keep the provisions of the said Act because, only through these provisions can the intent really be respected.
It is not the case here, Mr. Speaker. In this instance, and I am sure there was no mistake on the part of government, in the terms under which it can contract out services to a third party in an airport, the government did not make it mandatory to comply with the Official
Government Orders
Languages Act. The Official Languages Commissioner had to criticize the government saying that it contravenes the intent of the Official Languages Act of Canada.
When I took part in the proceedings of the committee that examined this bill, I asked to what extent the government could enforce the Official Languages Act if it was not specified in the bill. The answer I got is that it cannot be enforced and that it is left to the good will-quite an interesting phrase-to the good will of companies or individuals who will get the airport management contracts.
You should be wary of good will, Mr. Speaker. I heard that authorities who will be in charge of the Dorval airport expressed the view that they would not be able to compete with airports in Boston or New York if they had to comply with the Official Languages Act. It is a shame because it will create a system whereby workers in Dorval will not know what to do and passengers will have problems obtaining services in their own language, be it English or French, because there will be no obligation to provide services in both languages.
It is a shame because, when we studied the bill in committee, we tried to define which services should be provided in both languages, under the Official Languages Act, and which services could be provided in one language or the other. They said before the committee, Mr. Speaker, that only those services related to the act of travelling should be provided in both languages. It means that, if you have to eat in a restaurant, yes, you can be served in both languages, but if you want to buy an apple or an orange or if you want to have a haircut, those services do not have to be provided in both languages.
Then, they talked about places where one can order a drink, among other things. In such places, services might have to be offered in both languages. In fact, a real- how would I say-cacophony was heard from the committee trying to describe the services or the products to be available for sale in both languages.
Mr. Speaker, when people like my hon. friend from Edmonton-East say they have stood up for French in Alberta and are sorry that the Official Languages Act has not been respected, I think it is important. If people from Alberta and from across the country are saying: "Listen, we would like that law to be enforced", I think it is important and that the government should have considered including in the bill the enforcement of the

Mr. Speaker, in the short time I have today I would like to put on the record some important comments regarding questions I posed to the government specifically last Friday, and as well a similar question that
Adjournment Debate
I put today by chance to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It relates specifically to a veiy important issue in northern British Columbia in my riding. It is the whole question of a major hydroelectric project in my area commonly referred to as the Alcan project.
The question I put on Friday to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment and today to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans concerned the government's intent as it relates to a very important court ruling on May 16 of this year regarding this particular project. The Federal Court ruled that the Government of Canada must have an environmental assessment review of this Alcan project in northern B.C.
It is a very important ruling. There is a newspaper article on the ruling which quotes the decision of the judge in this case. It is an incredible indictment of this government's environmental policy and an indictment of the policy that this government has had over the last number of years as it relates to this entire project and its subsequent impact on the Nechako and Fraser Rivers.
The judge in this particular case declared, and I am quoting from the article in the newspaper, that the former environment minister's decision at that time to exempt this particular project from the full environmental assessment review process was "a failure to undertake a legal obligation". The judge certainly slapped, if not the government's wrist, the government around a bit and rightfully so. To not have an environmental assessment of this very major project draws into question this government's intent and its concern for the environment. It is also inconsistent with the announcement over the weekend of this government's plans under the green plan to tiy to clean up the Fraser River.
No plan to clean up and protect the Fraser River will be complete without a full environmental assessment of the Alcan project.
Just briefly, there are a couple of concerns that have been raised about this project that we have to repeat time and time again so that this government understands what it is a partner in. It is a partner in destroying the recreational fish habitat in the area, lowering the river flows, and increasing the temperature of the river affecting the salmon stocks in that particular area. It is a massive project that the government has allowed to continue.

June 3, 1991

So far to date, as recently as this afternoon, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has yet to make a decision about an environmental assessment review process.
It is critical and important, given all the evidence and information that has been made public about this project.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to inform the House that the Kemano hydroelectric project near Kitimat, British Columbia, was subject to detailed examination related to fisheries and other environmental issues.
The 1987 settlement agreement among Alcan Aluminium, the province of British Columbia and the federal government was a unique agreement providing an excellent example of sustainable development allowing economic development to proceed with ongoing implementation of mitigative measures as required.
Mitigation measures identified during environmental studies and a scientific inquiry by 10 experts chaired by Dr. David Strangway, President of the University of British Columbia, are being implemented by Alcan.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the province and the company continue to work through the mechanisms established by the agreement, such as the technical and steering committees to ensure that fishery matters are dealt with satisfactorily with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans monitoring the fisheries' mitigative measures to ensure their success.
The agreement among the province, Alcan and the federal government was based on several environmental considerations. Alcan prepared an extensive environmental impact report to describe the potential impacts of the project.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans carried out consultations to determine public concerns for impacts on fish and fish habitat, and government decisions were taken only after consideration of these impacts.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to inform the House that Department of Justice officials are actively involved in analysing the complex and numerous legal issues raised by the recent Federal Court decision regarding Alcan's Kemano project.
I am also pleased to inform the House that a full and proper interdepartmental consultation process is well under way to ensure that the many legal and policy considerations arising from the court's decision are carefully and thoroughly addressed.
A decision on whether to appeal the court's ruling will be made in the near future following the completion of this analysis.

Mr. Speaker, as my hon. colleague is well aware, the federal government continues to have a strong interest in the situation at Algoma Steel. We are particularly concerned for the future of the company and its workers and the possible impact on the people of Sault Ste. Marie.
Adjournment Debate
As the hon. member knows, in February of this year Dofasco announced that it was writing off its investment in Algoma and that the firm was on its own financially. At that time, Algoma announced that it would be meeting with its lenders to restructure its debts and begin operating under the company's Creditors Arrangements Act. This has afforded the company a measure of protection until July 31, 1991 to have financial arrangements worked out with all its lenders and creditors.
The federal government participated with the province of Ontario, Dofasco and the Royal Bank in providing Algoma with a $60 million loan guarantee. The federal government's share was $15 million. This guarantee, provided at commercial rates of interest, provided a bridge loan to allow the company to continue operating and meet its payroll and other financial obligations until it received the money for the sale of its coal mine properties in the United States. Before the end of March, Algoma had repaid this loan, and the federal government's financial commitment to the company ended.
The federal government is represented on the Algoma task force. It is composed of representatives of the federal government, the province, the banks, the employees, the suppliers and the community. While direct financial assistance to the contrary is not appropriate, the federal government will continue to work with Algoma and the other stakeholders to assist the firm in becoming more competitive.
In addition, federal efforts will include working with Algoma through External Affairs and International Trade Canada to develop new overseas markets for the company, identifying possible investors or partners for the company, and working with the community and the workers to help them adjust to the situation.
As to the employees of Algoma, the Canadian Steel Trade and Employment Congress has government funding and the mandate to assist laid off steel workers. In addition, the Community Futures Program of Employment and Immigration Canada has been operating successfully in the Soo since 1986.
The federal government has great interest in the Algoma situation and monitors the situation on a daily basis.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
We do not know whether there was a hockey game or any other activities. But, Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell you now about the long weekend in October, in the fall of 1989: it was a glorious weekend,
with beautiful fall leaves on the trees in Mont Royal park and elsewhere- But I know that the people involved did not use the weekend for the purpose of admiring nature, Mr. Speaker, they were too devoted to their work. Every apartment was occupied of course at 200 Saint-Marc Street, in Montreal, two blocks from Forum Street, but it was sheer coincidence.

The government has a housing policy, we have now discovered. It has a housing policy for Erik Nielsen and his friends at the National Transportation Agency; such a good housing policy that they get free housing when they go to Montreal.
I have the booking list here. It apparently is every now and then registered to guests. Who are those guests? Guests of whom? Why does the National Transportation Agency have an apartment in Montreal? Why does it have three apartments in Montreal? What is the purpose of this exercise? What does it cost the taxpayers, in addition to the $31,000 every nine months that it costs to rent the place, to administer the program?
I even have a sample form here of how you apply to use the fancy digs in Montreal if you happen to work at the National Transportation Agency or a as member of the board of the agency or others. Here is a request form: "Form for booking Montreal apartments, Part 1, general information, date, request submitted, requested by" and so on, "authorization from director, Part 2, confirmation". This is for the boss to say whether you can have the apartment in Montreal and so on.
The minister told us in the House she would investigate this, but I want to know what the answer is. What is the excuse for this abuse of taxpayers' money?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that after that entertaining interlude all of us would want to have the answer. In response to the hon. member's question I would like to put some facts before the House.
The National Transportation Agency has advised that it did rent three apartments in July 1989 in Montreal. One of the three apartments was used on an interim basis for an employee who was relocating to Montreal. It was cancelled when no longer needed.
June 3, 1991

The other two apartments were used for auditors travelling on a regular basis to Montreal to audit the books of CN and CP. One of those apartments was let go in April 1990.
The decision to rent the apartments rather than use hotels was made for a combination of reasons. First, economically it would provide a cost benefit to the National Transportation Agency. Second, it would ensure availability of space in Montreal. The hon. member may know often hotel rooms are difficult to locate, particularly during the convention season. Third, the location: the apartment offered affordable access from both the headquarters of CN and CP to the Montreal offices of the agency.
The use of the apartments was carefully monitored for the first four months and it was shown to provide a positive cost savings to the agency.
The accusations of the hon. member as to the luxuriousness of the apartments are quite exaggerated. A comparison with other similar apartment hotels in the government directory shows that this one comes in at the low end of the scale.
As she indicated in her response, the Minister of State for Transportation asked for a full review of this matter. A cost analysis indicates that there are no longer cost savings and thus the agency advises that it has cancelled the rental effective June 19.
The decision by the agency to rent this apartment was made by employees who were seeking a better solution to management problems, which is very much in keeping with Public Service 2000 philosophy.
I think that rather than criticizing the agency for this initiative, the member should be complimenting its employees on trying an innovative approach to solve a management problem.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief time that I have this evening, I want to expand a little bit on the question I posed to the minister of external affairs May 30.
At that time I was talking about the Al-Mashat affair and specifically about the differences between version a

and version b. I want to go back briefly because I think it is important for the House to know that version a of the Al-Mashat affair was provided to us at a press conference with great fanfare by the minister of external affairs and the minister of immigration, at which time they assured us that the matter was full and complete.
This was a report which contained four pages plus one paragraph. Is it my wording that says that the report was full and complete? It is not. On May 15, the day after the report was submitted, the hon. minister said: "A report was made. It is as complete as it can be and it tells people what they need to know". Lo and behold, two weeks later on May 30, another report was released-version b.
The first report was four pages and one paragraph. The second report was 26 pages. It does not take a mental giant to realize that there are additions and amplifications in version b. Are there any discrepancies? There are.
I chose to ask the minister about one of those discrepancies on May 30. At that time I pointed out specifically that on page 11 of version b, the report makes specific mention of a written memorandum dated March 8 which was prepared by the enforcement branch of Employment and Immigration Canada. It was to go to the minister of immigration. To say what? To advise of what was happening with the Al-Mashat application.
Interestingly enough, if you looked at version a you would find absolutely nothing whatsoever about that memorandum. It is not even mentioned. It is not even brought to our attention and yet we were assured by the minister of external affairs that the report was as complete as it could be and it told people what they needed to know.
Two weeks later, it seemed we needed to know more and so we got a little bit more.
What is even more troubling is the response that I received to my question. My question, very simply, was: Why is there something in version b that is not in version al What does the minister answer? I am quoting: "I am going to have all these documents in front of me before the committee. I will be very happy to answer all these questions, as I was this morning when-let the record show-this member" referring to me, "walked out too".
